articles.title: The pros and cons of using a MagSafe charger - Engadget
articles.text:
The pros and cons of using a MagSafe charger
Despite all of their conveniences, they're not perfect.
MagSafe as a technology actually dates all the way back to 2006, when Apple unveiled it as a magnetic power connector for the MacBook Pro. Apple ended up dropping the feature in favor of USB-C in 2015, but it eventually made its way back to the MacBook lineup.
You can still charge modern MacBooks through their USB-C ports at the same speeds you'd get with MagSafe, but you'll have to shop for a compatible USB-C cable separately. Apple bundles a USB-C to MagSafe cable with every MacBook, and it does offer its fair share of conveniences. For starters, charging your MacBook becomes as simple as bringing the MagSafe connector close to the charging port and letting the magnets snap it into place. Secondly, there's far less of a chance of your MacBook getting yanked off a desk if someone happens to accidentally trip over the charging cable — hence the name MagSafe.
As convenient as using a MagSafe cable for your MacBook is, it is a proprietary charging standard. This means you'll always be carrying around a dedicated cable that can't be used for anything other than charging your MacBook. A USB-C cable, on the other hand, can not only charge all of your devices, but it can also be used to connect external displays, hard drives and other peripherals to your Mac.
I remember almost exclusively using MagSafe for charging my MacBook when it was new and mostly docked at my desk, but the moment I started carrying it around, relying on USB-C just made more sense. It's also easier to justify buying newer USB-C cables since you know they'll come in handy for other devices, too.
What about MagSafe on iPhones?
Despite sharing the same name and technically offering the same magnetic convenience, MagSafe on the iPhone is a very different implementation from the connector that MacBooks use. For one, it's completely wireless. This means it cannot (yet) charge an iPhone as quickly or efficiently as a wired USB-C or Lightning connection can. If you own an iPhone 17e, iPhone 15 or an older model, MagSafe charging peaks at 15W, while newer models can wirelessly charge at up to 25W. With a compatible charger and USB-C cable, though, you can charge the iPhone 18 Pro much faster at up to 60W.
So, if you're looking for a quick top-up right before you head out, MagSafe may not be the most effective solution. Also, unlike the MacBook, Apple doesn't bundle a MagSafe charger with iPhones, so you'll have to pay extra for the convenience. That said, MagSafe on the iPhone goes beyond just wireless charging. You can buy magnetic wallets, phone stands, car mounts and other accessories that make good use of the magnets built into your iPhone.
MagSafe charging is still incredibly useful if you charge your phone overnight. You could have a wireless charging stand set up on your nightstand or at your desk and simply snap your iPhone onto it. Certain AirPods models that ship with a wireless charging case are also MagSafe-compatible and can be charged using the same magnetic charging accessories designed for the iPhone.

articles.title: Microsoft announces Windows and Surface event for October 7th
articles.text:
It’s been more than two years since the last major Windows event, so Microsoft is heading to San Francisco next month to outline the future of Windows and Surface devices. At an event on October 7th, the company says it will host a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC.”
Microsoft announces Windows and Surface event for October 7th
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella will be in attendance, alongside Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri. Even Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will be appearing at the event, which suggests that RTX Spark PCs could be the main focus of this event. If that’s the case, don’t be surprised to hear more about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra pricing and availability.
I am also expecting Microsoft to focus on its quality improvements to Windows, and what’s coming next. I am not expecting a surprise announce of Windows 12, though.
Microsoft last held a major Windows event in May 2024, to unveil new Arm-based Copilot Plus PCs and its renewed partnership with Qualcomm. The last major Windows event before that was in June 2021, when Microsoft announced Windows 11 during a live stream.
The Verge will be covering Microsoft’s Windows event next month live from San Francisco on October 7th at 10AM PT / 1PM ET.

articles.title: Cách gửi tiết kiệm 1 năm lấy lãi hàng tháng
articles.text:
Hiểu đúng về gửi tiết kiệm 1 năm lấy lãi hàng tháng
Gửi tiết kiệm kỳ hạn 1 năm lấy lãi hàng tháng là một sản phẩm tài chính được nhiều ngân hàng cung cấp, cho phép khách hàng gửi một khoản tiền cố định trong vòng 12 tháng và nhận tiền lãi đều đặn vào tài khoản mỗi tháng. Khác với hình thức gửi tiết kiệm truyền thống chỉ nhận lãi vào cuối kỳ, sản phẩm này mang lại sự linh hoạt đáng kể trong việc quản lý dòng tiền cá nhân.
Bản chất của hình thức này là ngân hàng sẽ tính toán tổng số tiền lãi dự kiến cho cả kỳ hạn 1 năm, sau đó chia nhỏ và thanh toán cho khách hàng theo từng tháng. Mức lãi suất thường được cố định ngay tại thời điểm gửi, giúp người gửi dễ dàng dự đoán được khoản thu nhập định kỳ của mình. Đây là một giải pháp tài chính hấp dẫn, đặc biệt với những ai có nhu cầu sử dụng một phần tiền lãi để chi tiêu hàng tháng hoặc tái đầu tư vào các kênh khác.
Lợi ích của hình thức gửi tiết kiệm này
Việc chọn gửi tiết kiệm 1 năm lấy lãi hàng tháng mang lại nhiều ưu điểm mà các hình thức khác khó có được:
Tạo dòng tiền đều đặn
Đây là lợi ích rõ ràng nhất. Thay vì phải chờ đến cuối kỳ hạn 1 năm mới nhận được toàn bộ tiền lãi, bạn sẽ có một khoản thu nhập bổ sung hàng tháng. Khoản tiền này có thể dùng để trang trải các chi phí sinh hoạt, đóng góp vào quỹ khẩn cấp, hoặc tái đầu tư ngay lập tức, giúp tối ưu hóa hiệu quả sử dụng vốn.
Quản lý tài chính linh hoạt hơn
Với tiền lãi nhận được hàng tháng, bạn có thể dễ dàng lập kế hoạch chi tiêu, đầu tư ngắn hạn hoặc tích lũy cho các mục tiêu khác mà không cần phải động đến số tiền gốc. Điều này giúp tăng cường khả năng kiểm soát tài chính cá nhân và giảm áp lực khi cần tiền đột xuất.
An toàn và ổn định
Giống như các hình thức tiết kiệm khác, gửi tiết kiệm 1 năm lấy lãi hàng tháng được bảo vệ bởi các quy định của Ngân hàng Nhà nước và chính sách bảo hiểm tiền gửi. Điều này đảm bảo an toàn cho khoản tiền gốc của bạn, ngay cả trong trường hợp ngân hàng gặp sự cố. Mức lãi suất cố định cũng giúp bạn tránh được những biến động thị trường, mang lại sự yên tâm tuyệt đối.
Khuyến khích thói quen tiết kiệm và đầu tư
Việc nhận lãi hàng tháng có thể là động lực để bạn duy trì thói quen tiết kiệm và thậm chí là tái đầu tư khoản lãi đó. Nếu bạn chọn tái đầu tư, hiệu ứng lãi kép sẽ giúp khoản tiền của bạn tăng trưởng nhanh hơn theo thời gian.
Quy trình gửi tiết kiệm 1 năm lấy lãi hàng tháng chi tiết
Quy trình gửi tiết kiệm thường khá đơn giản và nhanh chóng. Dưới đây là các bước cơ bản:
Bước 1: Chuẩn bị hồ sơ
Bạn cần chuẩn bị các giấy tờ tùy thân hợp lệ như:
- Chứng minh nhân dân/Căn cước công dân còn hiệu lực.
- Nếu là người nước ngoài, cần có hộ chiếu và giấy tờ chứng minh cư trú hợp pháp tại Việt Nam.
Bước 2: Lựa chọn hình thức gửi
Bạn có thể chọn gửi tiết kiệm tại quầy giao dịch hoặc gửi tiết kiệm online (nếu ngân hàng có hỗ trợ).
- Tại quầy giao dịch: Đến chi nhánh ngân hàng gần nhất, điền vào phiếu gửi tiền và các biểu mẫu liên quan. Nhân viên ngân hàng sẽ hỗ trợ bạn hoàn tất thủ tục.
- Gửi online: Đăng nhập vào ứng dụng ngân hàng hoặc website của ngân hàng, chọn mục gửi tiết kiệm, điền thông tin và xác nhận giao dịch. Hình thức này tiện lợi, nhanh chóng và thường có lãi suất cạnh tranh.
Bước 3: Ký kết hợp đồng và nhận sổ/xác nhận
Sau khi hoàn tất thủ tục, bạn sẽ nhận được sổ tiết kiệm (nếu gửi tại quầy) hoặc xác nhận giao dịch điện tử (nếu gửi online). Hãy kiểm tra kỹ các thông tin trên sổ/xác nhận, đặc biệt là số tiền gửi, kỳ hạn, lãi suất và ngày đáo hạn.
Bước 4: Theo dõi và quản lý
Ngân hàng sẽ tự động chuyển tiền lãi vào tài khoản của bạn hàng tháng. Bạn có thể theo dõi các giao dịch này qua sao kê tài khoản, ứng dụng ngân hàng hoặc internet banking. Đến cuối kỳ hạn 1 năm, số tiền gốc sẽ được hoàn trả vào tài khoản của bạn hoặc tự động tái tục theo thỏa thuận ban đầu.

articles.title: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google have been in talks on AI safety for weeks | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s global policy chief, told reporters on Tuesday that the company has been working with rivals Anthropic and Google DeepMind on AI safety for weeks, as first reported by Bloomberg. Lehane is reportedly in Washington to work with U.S. lawmakers addressing catastrophic risks associated with AI.
The revelation comes in the wake of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay, published Saturday, which called for the industry to work together to slow the pace of frontier AI and avoid catastrophic risks. AI leaders across the industry, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google’s Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, supported Amodei’s letter and call to action, with Altman saying that OpenAI would join Anthropic in embedding third-party evaluators into the company to monitor for safety.
On Tuesday, Lehane admitted that the three companies have been in talks for several weeks regarding AI safety. Some, including Altman, have noted that such talks could put the companies at risk of violating antitrust law if the coordination is found to suppress competition. Amodei’s essay proposed a narrow government waiver allowing such safety coordination, but Lehane reportedly said the firms don’t need one.
The news confirms earlier reporting and hints that the companies were working together. In an interview with Fortune late last week, Altman hinted that he had been in private discussions with other AI leaders. This week, The Information reported that the three companies have been working together to create a standards body for the AI industry — something Altman reportedly told staff would need to happen without the support of the U.S. government.
Hassabis called on the U.S. in July to establish a new standards body to act as an AI watchdog, with the power to screen the world’s most advanced models and coordinate industrywide slowdowns if dangers progressed.
President Trump, for his part, has dismissed safety concerns as a hoax and pushed back on the need for tighter regulations, saying any slowdown would give China a leg up in the race. His key AI advisor David Sacks — a longtime investor with a personal stake in much of the industry — echoed this, saying fears of existential risk from AI were overblown.
At the same Tuesday meeting, Lehane said that OpenAI supports a provision in the FRONTIER Act that would force top frontier labs to allow “independent verification organizations” into their companies to ensure models are developed safely.
TechCrunch has reached out to Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI for comment.

articles.title: Spotify can now exclude your kids' music taste from recommendations - Engadget
articles.text:
Spotify can now exclude your kids' music taste from recommendations
The end of Disney songs popping up in your Daily Mix.
Just because you have to listen to "Let It Go" for the zillionth time while driving your kids to school doesn't mean it should dominate your Spotify Wrapped. The streaming service is adding a new toggle option for users to exclude certain kids or family songs from affecting your music recommendations, like nursery rhymes, TV show theme songs or musical hits from animated movies.
Within the settings panel, there's now a new toggle labeled "Include kids and family music in taste profile" that will change what shows up in your Discovery Weekly, Daily Mix or Wrapped. Like the Explicit content switch, Spotify has a note that says it could "take up to 48 hours for these changes to be reflected in your personalized recommendations." However, activating the kid and family music toggle will also work retroactively, meaning that all the relevant music you listened to this year can still be wiped away from your annual Wrapped recap. The feature is available to both Free and Premium users.
The latest toggle option builds on Spotify's Managed accounts feature that was introduced in 2025 to give kid accounts that are part of a shared family plan a space to listen to their own music and prevent it from affecting other accounts' taste profiles. Before introducing managed accounts, Spotify added the ability to exclude playlists from user's taste profiles, and later added a feature that can hide individual tracks in 2025.

articles.title: OpenAI's head of countries says Canada has the energy and land for data centres
articles.text:
OpenAI is looking at data centre partnerships in Canada because of the energy and land available there, its head of countries George Osborne told Bloomberg at Mark Carney’s investment summit in Toronto. OpenAI paused its British project in April, saying it would proceed when regulation and the cost of energy allowed.
OpenAI is looking at data centre partnerships in Canada because of the energy and land available there, its head of countries George Osborne told Bloomberg. He was speaking at Mark Carney’s investment summit in Toronto.
Osborne was Britain’s chancellor from 2010 to 2016. In 2012 he hired Carney, then governor of the Bank of Canada, to run the Bank of England.
He joined OpenAI in December as managing director and head of OpenAI for Countries, the arm that takes the Stargate model abroad. He works from London.
Carney has articulated “one of the clearer plans for AI adoption of a western government“, Osborne said, calling the prime minister’s medium and long-term plan “very impressive“.
The summit ran on 14 and 15 September and brought about 100 of the world’s largest investment firms to Toronto. Carney wants to catalyse a trillion dollars of investment over five years.
Europe got a different answer.
OpenAI paused Stargate UK in April, saying it would move forward when regulation and the cost of energy allowed long-term infrastructure investment. The project was to run 8,000 Nvidia GPUs in the north east of England, scaling to 31,000.
British industrial electricity costs roughly four times what it does in the United States, Finland, Norway and Sweden. Grid connection requests jumped from 41 gigawatts in November 2024 to 125 gigawatts by June 2025.
The announcement did not survive much scrutiny either. OpenAI had never visited the site of its flagship British project, the Guardian found, and the government had publicised a GBP 1.9B contract that was not signed.
The copyright question is still open. A proposed text and data mining exception met opposition from the creative industries, and no law has followed.
Where OpenAI did build in Europe was Norway. Stargate Norway runs on Narvik hydropower, 230 megawatts to start, with 100,000 Nvidia GPUs targeted by the end of this year.
Energy and land, in other words. The same two things Osborne named in Toronto.
The EU is trying to buy its way past the problem, with a gigafactories call that closes to bids on 12 November and expects more than EUR 20B of private investment across up to seven sites. France’s $10B bid is already in.

Giá vàng thế giới hôm nay 15/9/2026
Lúc gần 8h sáng 15/9 (giờ Việt Nam), giá vàng giao ngay trên Kitco ở mức 4.293,10 USD/ounce, giảm 5,10 USD, tương đương 0,12% so với mức tham chiếu. Trong phiên, giá vàng dao động trong khoảng 4.253-4.356,30 USD/ounce.
Trước đó, vàng có thời điểm giảm xuống mức thấp nhất hơn một tháng. Trong phiên 14/9, giá vàng giao ngay giảm 0,8% xuống 4.312,59 USD/ounce vào lúc 13h30 giờ miền Đông nước Mỹ. Giá vàng kỳ hạn Mỹ giảm 1,3%, xuống 4.351,90 USD/ounce.
Kim loại quý chịu sức ép khi giá dầu tăng mạnh làm gia tăng lo ngại lạm phát, qua đó củng cố kỳ vọng Fed sẽ thắt chặt chính sách tiền tệ. Đồng USD mạnh lên và lợi suất trái phiếu Mỹ tăng cũng làm giảm sức hấp dẫn của vàng - tài sản không sinh lãi.
Lúc 21h30 ngày 14/9 (giờ Việt Nam), giá vàng giao ngay ở mức khoảng 4.270 USD/ounce, giảm 79 USD. Giá vàng kỳ hạn tháng 11/2026 ở mức 4.312 USD/ounce.
Thị trường tiếp tục phản ứng với số liệu lạm phát Mỹ công bố cuối tuần trước. CPI tháng 8 tăng 0,4% so với tháng trước, đưa mức tăng theo năm lên 3,4%. CPI lõi tăng 0,3%, cao hơn mức dự báo 0,2%.
Kết hợp với giá năng lượng tăng cao, số liệu này khiến thị trường nâng xác suất Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) tăng lãi suất 0,25 điểm phần trăm trong cuộc họp ngày 16-17/9 lên khoảng 87%. Thị trường cũng dự báo tổng mức tăng lãi suất trong 12 tháng tới có thể hơn 90 điểm cơ bản.
Lợi suất trái phiếu Kho bạc Mỹ kỳ hạn 10 năm tăng lên gần 4,97%, sau khi có thời điểm chạm 4,992%, cao nhất gần 3 năm và tiến sát ngưỡng 5%. Lợi suất cao làm tăng chi phí cơ hội nắm giữ vàng, vốn không sinh lãi, qua đó gây sức ép lên giá kim loại quý.
Tâm lý người tiêu dùng Mỹ suy yếu. Chỉ số niềm tin người tiêu dùng của Đại học Michigan giảm từ 51,7 điểm trong tháng 8 xuống 47,8 điểm trong tháng 9. Kỳ vọng lạm phát trong một năm tới tăng từ 4% lên 4,6%, còn kỳ vọng dài hạn tăng từ 3,3% lên 3,4%.
Áp lực từ thị trường trái phiếu vẫn là yếu tố đáng chú ý đối với vàng trong ngắn hạn. Nợ công Mỹ đã vượt 40.000 tỷ USD, trong khi lợi suất cao làm gia tăng chi phí trả nợ của Chính phủ. Nếu lợi suất trái phiếu kỳ hạn 10 năm duy trì trên 5%, chi phí vay có thể tiếp tục tăng và gây thêm sức ép lên tài khóa Mỹ.
Bất ổn địa chính trị tại Trung Đông tiếp tục hỗ trợ nhu cầu trú ẩn, nhưng đồng thời khiến giá năng lượng tăng mạnh. Các cuộc tấn công nhằm vào cơ sở hạ tầng năng lượng và hoạt động vận tải biển làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguồn cung dầu.
Giá dầu Brent vượt 108 USD/thùng, còn WTI duy trì trên 100 USD/thùng.
Dự báo giá vàng
Adrian Day, Chủ tịch Adrian Day Asset Management, cho rằng việc vàng giữ được sức mạnh khi lạm phát tiêu dùng Mỹ tăng, lợi suất trái phiếu Kho bạc đi lên và kỳ vọng Fed tăng lãi suất được củng cố là tín hiệu tích cực. Giá vàng có thể đang hình thành vùng giá nền mới quanh 4.300 USD/ounce trước khi tăng trở lại.
Rich Checkan, Chủ tịch kiêm Giám đốc điều hành Asset Strategies International, cho rằng các số liệu lạm phát gần đây chưa tạo ra tín hiệu đủ mạnh để Fed nhất thiết phải tăng lãi suất.
Bob Haberkorn, chuyên gia môi giới hàng hóa cấp cao tại StoneX Group, nhận định dư địa giảm của vàng đang bị hạn chế do khả năng lãi suất tăng mạnh là không lớn. Nhà đầu tư đang thận trọng chờ quyết định của Fed, trong khi lực mua bắt đáy đã xuất hiện nhưng chưa mạnh.
Theo Haberkorn, nếu Fed không tăng lãi suất, giá vàng có thể tăng đáng kể trong những tháng cuối năm và hướng tới mốc 5.000 USD/ounce. Ngược lại, nếu Fed tăng 0,25 điểm phần trăm, vàng có thể điều chỉnh nhưng mức giảm nhiều khả năng không quá sâu do dư địa nâng lãi suất của Fed bị hạn chế bởi nợ công cao và tác động lên nền kinh tế.

articles.title: Those Viral Bodega Peptides Aren’t Actually Peptides
articles.text:
The Mr. Green bodega sits on a busy stretch of Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn, New York. Near the counter, you can buy the usual assortment of candy, gum, rolling papers, and soda. You can also purchase tiny vials of injectable peptides. So we did. And then we sent them to a lab.
Mr. Green is one of several shops that went viral this summer for selling peptides, a broad class of amino acids touted for their ability to aid in everything from weight loss to injury recovery. For $376.20, we acquired four varieties from a vendor called INDR Labs: PT-141, for low libido; BPC-157, for healing and muscle recovery; NAD+, for cellular repair; and retatrutide, for weight loss. The clerk packed them up in an unlabeled paper bag and sent us on our way.
WIRED sent the vials to Finnrick, an Austin-based startup that offers independent peptide testing. Consumers can request tests for purity and whether samples contain common contaminants, as well as whether they contain the quantity of the substance listed. The company doesn’t have in-house labs but instead acts as a middleman between labs and individuals. In a few weeks’ time, Finnrick told us, we’d know if our bodega peptides were the real deal.
In August, the results came in. The (relatively) good news: The samples contained low levels of heavy metals and endotoxins, meaning they likely weren’t actively harmful. The bad news: They weren’t peptides.
The testing for each substance found that they did not contain the active ingredients on their labels—the BPC-157, for example, had no BPC-157 within it. The negative results suggested that the vials were either mislabeled or, if they had at one point contained the correct ingredients, had been corrupted beyond recognition. Peptides are often sensitive to temperature changes and require refrigeration, so improper storage could degrade ingredients, for example.
What did they contain? Hard to say, according to Marco Krause, the chief executive officer of the laboratory that performed the tests for Finnrick.
“What we offer is simply a label claim analysis. So you send us what you claim to think it is, and then we run it against a standard and verify whether or not it's the right compound,” he tells WIRED.
Peptides have surged in popularity in recent years, powered by endorsements from figures like US health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and podcaster Joe Rogan. While some of these substances are pharmaceutical drugs like GLP-1s and insulin, many of the buzziest peptides have not been put through the typical regulatory approval process for drugs. Despite the hype surrounding them, many of these substances are not legal to sell for human consumption in the US—some precisely because they haven’t gone through the drug approval pipeline—and evidence of their purported benefits is thin.
The sign at Mr. Green advertising the peptides noted they were for “research use only,” a term that labs can use in an attempt to shield themselves from legal liability. But as the test results show, there’s no guarantee what’s in the vials—and in some cases there are real dangers to those taking them.
According to Raphaël Mazoyer, Finnrick’s CEO, the samples WIRED tested appear to be “just duds.” Over the past three months, Mazoyer says, the company has seen an uptick in these kinds of results. Though he can’t say for certain what’s going on—in part, his company has been testing more samples as it has grown—he points to the popularity of so-called turnkey services, which help pretty much anyone open a peptide business.
“There are a whole bunch of labels popping up that have the same upstream vendor,” he says. Not all the peptides Finnrick tests are duds, but the nature of the industry means that businesses may use the same shoddy supplier across a number of different brands.
WIRED isn’t the only organization to receive abnormal lab results after sending in peptides sold over the counter. Jeff Colhoun, the founder of the research-peptide vendor directory Peptide Critic, purchased INDR Labs peptides from a smoke shop down the street from Mr. Green called Smoker’s World and sent them to a different independent laboratory for testing.
Colhoun purchased two vials of retatrutide and two vials of NAD+ and had all four analyzed by Texas-based Analytical Formulations. The lab could “not positively identify” the substances. This doesn’t mean that they didn’t contain any of the substances listed, but it does suggest that the samples may have been contaminated or were otherwise too corrupted to decipher what was in the vials.
Colhoun says that he has heard from research-peptide vendors who have had similar results while testing products prior to selling them, and notes that buyers are at a high risk level when sellers “skip meaningful batch testing” altogether.
INDR Labs did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment, but shortly after we reached out, its website began requiring login credentials. It previously cut off public access to its certificates of analysis, which provide evidence that a product has met certain standards. The company claimed its certificates were provided by Vanguard Laboratory; a spokesperson for Vanguard denied issuing the paperwork, CBS News previously reported.
INDR Labs is just one part of this booming ecosystem that investors estimate is already worth up to $3 billion, according to reporting from Bloomberg News. While the FDA has taken recent steps to loosen regulations, and many large telehealth platforms like Hims and Mochi are preparing to start selling a broad array of peptides, many people who take these substances today are purchasing them through questionable channels.
“The FDA needs to shut down these black markets,” Fred Mills, a longtime pharmacist and an executive at the nonprofit Americans for Safe and Effective Medicines, tells WIRED. Mills, who is based in Louisiana, says he’s had discussions recently about the dangers of people purchasing peptide products at convenience stores and that he warns those who do so to consult with a physician first.
If a peptide vial actually contains little more than water or saline solution, the worst that might happen is that someone loses money on a useless product. But some mislabeled peptides can contain ingredients that cause harm; a woman died this year after receiving a peptide injection from an unlicensed medical spa in the Bronx.
“My concern with the peptide industry is, we're legitimizing products, and we have no idea what's in them. We have no idea about the safety, accuracy profile, or whether they're adulterated or misbranded,” says Darshan Kulkarni, an attorney focused on pharmaceutical regulatory compliance. In the traditional pharmaceutical sales world, steps are taken to ensure prescription accuracy and product safety, from visual inspections to barcoding.
“Someone selling a product at a bodega doesn't know how to do that,” Kulkarni says.
“The FDA has warned companies selling products labeled ‘for research purposes’ or ‘not for human consumption’ when those products are marketed directly to consumers for human use,” an agency spokesperson who declined to give their name tells WIRED in an email. “Additionally, the FDA has warned telehealth companies for marketing drugs directly to consumers and for making false or misleading claims regarding compounded GLP-1 products offered on their websites. The FDA will continue to take action, where appropriate, to protect public health.”
The agency did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it has contacted or taken enforcement action against brick-and-mortar sellers of peptides labeled research-only, like those sold by Mr. Green.
There have been some enforcement actions. Earlier this summer, a man in South Bend, Indiana, was sentenced to six years in prison for selling “research use” peptides that were illegally imported from China—a major source of peptide ingredients—and were adulterated with steroids. Still, the enforcement atmosphere is loose enough that it remains easy to buy unapproved peptides both online and at brick-and-mortar medspas and other locations.
Kulkarni believes that the relatively low number of enforcement actions taken against the research peptide industry is related to the Trump administration’s attitude that “regulation stifles innovation, and therefore they believe that it is in the interest of patients to allow them to decide what products to take.”
As for Mr. Green, it did not respond to a written list of questions provided by WIRED. When we visited in early September, the menu in the window advertising the peptides was gone. But a smaller version was next to the counter, and the peptides were still for sale.
Additional reporting by Caroline Haskins.

articles.title: What if social media isn’t hurting kids?
articles.text:
Two years ago, social psychologist Jonathan Haidt released his New York Times bestseller The Anxious Generation. The book posits that the rise of social media and smartphone use is largely to blame for the prominent decline in teen mental health since 2010. It quickly became a central rallying cry of the social media backlash. Haidt has been credited with helping inspire Australia’s nationwide teen social media ban. He has joined forces with bereaved parents who are fighting tech companies in court. His name comes up unprompted in conversations with people in power who say his book opened their eyes to an online crisis.
What if social media isn’t hurting kids?
A new book says modern schooling, not phones, are behind youth mental health declines. Will anyone listen?
Haidt’s theory has received regular critiques from recognized academics. Candice Odgers, a leading adolescent mental health researcher, wrote a scathing review of Haidt’s analysis in Nature that opened by conceding, “this book is going to sell a lot of copies, because Jonathan Haidt is telling a scary story about children’s development that many parents are primed to believe.” Now, in the wake of that highly accurate prediction, a former colleague of Haidt’s seeks to not only take down his theory, but also offer an alternative. The biggest question may not be whether he’s correct — but whether it’s too late to change course if he is.
In his new book Restoring Childhood, psychology researcher Peter Gray argues that teens’ mental health declined thanks to decades of steadily reduced autonomy, and after a brief period of reprieve, fell again in the 2010s not — as Haidt argues — because of phones and social media, but because of rigid schooling methods linked to the Common Core curriculum and government pressure to improve children’s performance. And far from being damaging, Gray also argues the adoption of home internet in the 1990s and 2000s actually drove a rebound in teens’ mental health by restoring freedom and connection lost in earlier decades. He fears social media bans aren’t just — as Odgers has argued — a distraction from real solutions, but a new harm in themselves.
“You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy”
In an interview on The Vergecast, Gray told me that Haidt’s book “completely ignored” dozens of meta-analyses and other research that’s found “not even a meaningful correlation between the amount of time kids are on social media or on smartphones and their mental health.” Where there is some connection, Gray adds, studies suggest that teens may use social media to cope with their depression or anxiety. He references a study in Florida that found 11-to-13-year-olds who owned smartphones were more likely to spend real-world time with friends. “You take a smartphone away from your kids and that study suggests you’ll make them less happy and they’ll have less friends,” he says.
Gray says that in studies through the years, kids consistently identify school pressure, not social media, as their top source of anxiety. “That doesn’t mean it’s the primary source for everybody, but when you’re looking at the population at large, every single study that I’ve been able to find where kids are asked, ‘What’s the primary source of your anxiety or your stress or your depression?’, in every single one of them, school pressure comes out on top,” Gray tells me. “Nothing else comes close.”
Gray and Haidt both believe that since at least the 1980s, increased restrictions on kids’ independence and unstructured play have damaged their resilience. While it used to be common for kids to play together unsupervised, that practice has diminished in part due to the rise of “stranger danger” narratives fostered by rare, but high-profile, crimes. In 2017 the pair helped cofound an organization called Let Grow, which advocates for policies that make it easier for parents to let their children play freely, like ensuring they can’t be considered neglectful for letting kids outside by themselves. But the two have split sharply over the impact of the internet. Gray’s book is intended as a deliberate rebuttal to Haidt’s — after The Anxious Generation’s release, Gray resigned from the board of Let Grow to avoid conflict within the organization.
Haidt did not respond to a request for comment from The Verge, but he told The Atlantic’s Kaitlyn Tiffany in a July article that the 1990s and early 2000s dip in teen suicide rates may be credited to a phase-out of leaded gasoline, since lead exposure has been linked to mental health issues. He also told Tiffany that Gray relied too heavily on a minority dissenting group of researchers. Tiffany writes that many of the more than a dozen tech and child development researchers she spoke to “expressed concern that Haidt overstates the strength of correlational findings and suggests causation where it hasn’t been proved.”
Gray accuses Haidt of stirring a moral panic over technology that isn’t, on the whole, harmful. Looking across research, he says, Common Core is the clearest explanation for the sudden decline in teen mental health. And at the population level, the impact of social media “balances out. Some kids are doing better, some kids are doing worse because they’re on social media.”
“We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots”
Gray says he’s not opposed to all guardrails, including school phone bans and the concept of age verification for accessing pornography. But he questions the effectiveness of bans on social media, knowing kids are likely to get around them, and is hesitant to restrict platforms that let kids express themselves — suggesting instead that parents focus on teaching their children to navigate them. “We need to stop treating kids as if they’re idiots,” he told me. “We need to start understanding that kids are pretty good at knowing what’s good for them and not good for them and they can benefit from our help in learning how to do these things.”
But increasingly, parents of younger teens may not have that choice. Haidt’s theory holds undisputed dominance in many circles, including among politicians. Since Australia’s social media ban for teens, the UK and European Union are among those considering their own bans or platform limits. In the US, states like California and New York have enacted limits on certain social media features, and a federal proposal would restrict algorithmic feeds for kids under 17. Even among people who find Gray’s arguments about Common Core convincing, some might still see taking kids offline as a harmless precaution.
With so much momentum behind the backlash against phones and social media, can Gray’s book still make a difference? “I certainly hope it’s not too late,” he says. He points out that some moral panics have petered out. In the 1990s and 2000s, for instance, many people worried that video games like Mortal Kombat and Doom were making kids more violent, connecting their rise to that of school shootings. Eventually, research showed many mass shooters didn’t play video games after all. Attempts at regulation — including a California ban on the sale of violent games to children — were largely overruled. And many kids who did play them grew up to become those in charge. “The science won out eventually,” Gray says. “So it’s not me that’s going to win out. It’s the science that’s going to win out.”

articles.title: AEO startup Profound hits unicorn valuation, raises $180M Series D 7 months after last round | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Profound, which builds marketing software to help brands appear in AI search results, on Tuesday said it has raised a $180 million Series D at a $1.8 billion valuation, less than seven months after it raised a $96 million Series C.
Sequoia and Kleiner Perkins led the round, and existing investors — including Lightspeed Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures, and South Park Commons — also participated.
Launched two years ago, Profound started as an analytics platform, and has since expanded to help companies research and create marketing strategies. The startup helps businesses understand how AI helps consumers discover their brands.
It’s part of a wave of startups in the GEO/AEO space (generative engine optimization and answer engine optimization, respectively), where companies try to find ways to surface their products in the AI systems customers are increasingly using for search.
The company says its revenue has increased by 3x in the past six months, and it now has more than 1,000 enterprise customers, which include Comcast, The Estée Lauder Companies, and Walmart.

articles.title: "I am the Hoax Buster," Trump says of AI safety fears
articles.text:
Donald Trump has called fears about AI a “HOAX” in a string of Truth Social posts. The US president also asked why AI industry leaders want to be regulated. The posts came a day after his remarks in Ireland, where he called people asking to slow AI down a negative force.
“Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?” Trump wrote on Monday, 14 September.
In the same post, he said fears of AI “destroying Humanity” were a hoax. He compared them to the Russia investigation, Ukraine, and his two impeachments.
What Trump wrote
That post also made claims about China and Google. Trump wrote that Chinese President Xi Jinping had “just announced” that China would do nothing to stand in the way of AI. He did not say where Xi said this.
Trump also wrote that Google wants to build “a massive Plant in Finland” because permitting is too difficult in the US. “I am not happy about this, and want them to change their thinking,” he added.
Google said last week that it would invest €13bn in four Finnish data centre sites. Trump did not cite a Google statement for his claim about permitting.
He called AI and data centres “the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History”. He wrote that they would be bigger than oil, gold, diamonds, or the internet, and would not be stopped during his term.
In a later post, Trump linked AI warnings to climate change warnings. He said the same people were behind both, and called them “Revolutionaries for a Bad and Evil Cause”. “Soon you’ll find out they’re working for people that do not have the best interests of the United States in mind!” he wrote.
Three more posts followed that evening. In the first, Trump called himself “the Hoax Buster”. He mocked the idea of robots “marching into our Cities”.
In the second, he again called the claim that AI will take over the world a hoax. He said the people behind it were “Radical Left Dumocrats, who never give up, but seldom win.” In the third, he compared the “AI Hoax” to what he called “their Global Warming Scam”.
Earlier posts and Amodei
Earlier on Monday, Trump wrote that AI’s only “guardrails” should be “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”, Politico reported. He also described a “SICK conspiracy” against AI and data centres. China was the only one happy about it, he wrote.
Trump also named Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei. He wrote that Amodei was now pretending to be “a ‘perfect little angel’”, Business Insider reported. One post ended with a warning to “Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers”.
Over the weekend, Amodei called for the industry to slow down in an essay. Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman backed the call. Anthropic did not immediately respond to Politico or Business Insider.
The administration and Anthropic have clashed before. The Pentagon blacklisted the company after a contract dispute. A federal judge later struck down the blacklist. This month, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Axios that the administration trusts Anthropic, Business Insider reported.
On Monday, Trump also phoned Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who was on stage at the All-In Summit. On the call, Trump again called AI fears a hoax.
Vance and Johnson
Vice President JD Vance spoke to reporters on Monday. He said he felt “a little bit weird” about AI companies asking to be regulated. “It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse,” he said, according to Politico. Americans should be mindful of the risks, but not scared, he added.
House Speaker Mike Johnson echoed the president on Tuesday. “What the president is saying is, you’re not all going to be dead in 10 years. That’s a hoax,” he said, Courthouse News reported.
Johnson said AI companies must make safe products and can regulate themselves. He opposed a moratorium on AI development, saying the US would lose its edge to China. He also plans to meet the heads of the major AI labs.
Democrats and Congress
Democrats criticised the posts. Senator Chris Coons said Trump’s attacks on Americans worried about AI showed he does not understand the moment, Politico reported. Coons called for Congress to act.
Senator Ted Cruz chairs the Senate Commerce Committee. He may hold a markup on AI bills this month, according to Politico. One is a bill on biological and nuclear threats that he is drafting with Senators Amy Klobuchar and John Thune.
A University of Massachusetts Amherst poll was published on Monday. It found that 57% of Americans are unhappy with Trump’s handling of AI, and 23% are in favour, The Independent reported.

articles.title: The Census Bureau Is Overrun With Staffers From a MAGA Think Tank
articles.text:
Multiple staffers at a Trump-aligned policy think tank have burrowed their way into the US Census Bureau, where they have access to sensitive data and have contributed to a public report that bolsters conspiracy theories undermining trust in elections ahead of the midterms.
In August, the Census Bureau published an anonymously authored report titled “Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis,” claiming to show that thousands of noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. A WIRED investigation revealed that the report appeared to employ faulty methodology, casting its conclusions into doubt, and that two of its authors work for the America First Policy Institute, a right-wing think tank with deep ties to the Trump administration. Now WIRED has found that the two authors are part of a larger team, made up almost entirely of AFPI members, who have been detailed to the Census Bureau and given access to its data.
The Census Bureau is home to vast troves of sensitive data on nearly every person living in the country, which is used for apportioning and drawing congressional districts as well as allocating federal funding based on population sizes. Experts and Census employees who spoke to WIRED worry that the noncitizen voting report is the first salvo in Census data possibly being used to undermine the results of the upcoming midterms or the 2028 presidential election.
A Census employee who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity says that there has historically been “nothing close” to what AFPI is doing at the bureau. “Frankly, it's disrespectful to the institution,” they say.
The Trump administration has repeatedly attempted to cast doubt on the accuracy of Census data in order to reshape elections. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that the Department of Commerce, which oversees the bureau, was circulating a rule change that would eliminate noncitizens from being counted in the Census, a move that could drastically reshape how Congressional districts are drawn. Republicans also took aim at a little-known statistical method called differential privacy that is used to protect the privacy of individual respondents, alleging that it makes the Census count inaccurate in ways that favor Democrats in congressional apportionment.
AFPI, meanwhile, has been integral to shaping the Trump administration’s policies and makeup. Brooke Rollins, who served as the group’s first CEO, is now the secretary of agriculture, and Linda McMahon, now the secretary of education, used to sit on the organization’s board. Former AFPI staffers have found their way to some of the highest ranks of the Trump administration, including former attorney general Pam Bondi, secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins, secretary of Housing and Urban Development Scott Turner, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin, US permanent representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, deputy director of White House Domestic Policy Council Heidi Overton, and National Economic Council of the United States director Kevin Hassett.
In addition to Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea, the two AFPI members previously identified by WIRED, at least five other AFPI members have been or are currently staffed at the Census Bureau, according to sources and documents reviewed by WIRED. Sources who spoke to WIRED confirmed that all the AFPI members are detailed to the agency through the Intergovernmental Personnel Act (IPA), which allows people with specialized skills from certain institutions, like nonprofits and universities, to work for the government for up to two years on a temporary appointment.
The Census Bureau and AFPI did not respond to requests for comment.
John Abowd, former associate director for research and methodology and chief scientist at the Census Bureau, says that having so many people from a single organization would be “unusual.”
Among the names viewed by WIRED are Max Kossek, a researcher at AFPI’s Office for Fiscal and Regulatory Analysis, and Ryan Montgomery, who the website lists as a program assistant with the same AFPI office. Montgomery’s LinkedIn profile, however, says that he is now a “research engineer” at AFPI.
AFPI’s director for secure elections policy, Thomas Lane, is also listed as one of the employees that has been detailed to the Census Bureau. Lane, a former Trump campaign staffer and election denier, was subpoenaed by the Department of Justice in 2022 as part of its investigation into the president’s attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election. (Lane was not charged by law enforcement.) In a 2020 video posted by the Arizona Republican Party, where a group of fake electors attempted to deliver the state’s electoral votes to Donald Trump, Politico identified a man wearing a jacket with the name “Lane” on it passing out the documents for the electors to sign making them “duly elected” and “qualified.” In 2024, CNN reported that Lane was prepared to serve as a backup elector for that same group.
Earlier this year, Democracy Docket reported that Lane helped write part of an early version of the Save America Act, the law that would require voter ID to register to vote, while working for the Republican majority House Committee on House Administration. Parts of the Save Act have also been included in the separate Save America Act, which, if passed, would require proof of citizenship in order to vote, a move that experts say could disenfranchise more than 20 million people.
Kossek, Montgomery, and Lane did not respond to requests for comment.
David Peterson, who AFPI lists as a research engineer with expertise in “computing, machine learning, and advanced software architecture,” and Jackson Mejia, an AFPI fellow who is an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin with a PhD in economics from MIT focusing on tax policy, also appear to be detailed to the Census Bureau. Peterson and Mejia did not respond to requests for comment.
Another person, listed as an IPA from AFPI, Michael Corey, is also listed among the group at the bureau. AFPI does not list Corey as a staff member on its website, but an AFPI email with Corey’s name does appear to exist. AFPI did not confirm whether Corey was currently associated with the think tank.
Danah Boyd, a professor at Cornell University who studies the census, says that there are vehicles like the American Association for the Advancement of Science through which agencies like the Census Bureau might bring in multiple IPAs. But AFPI, Boyd says, “is not an institution that is set up to bring all the scientists in the world together or that has built this long-standing infrastructure of doing independent statistical research. This is a partisan group with an agenda,” she claims.
All of the AFPI members are listed under the same project, focused on “ad hoc data analyses” to answer questions from senior leaders at Census and the Department of Commerce, according to documentation viewed by WIRED. The project appears to be led by Michael Lachanski, the bureau’s recently appointed deputy director for data, policy, and science, and a former fellow at the Claremont Institute, a conservative think tank that also has connections to the Trump administration. Lachanski is a political appointee. All of the AFPI detailees appear to have the “special sworn status” necessary to access sensitive Census data.
Recent reporting from Talking Points Memo found that the Census Bureau’s Data Stewardship Executive Policy charter had been updated in July to remove stipulations that prevented political appointees from interfering with the bureau’s data.
Another Census employee, who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the press, says that access to Census data is only allowed through approved “projects,” where employees and researchers have to explain how they're going to use the data and what they're going to produce. The employee says that it’s not unheard of to have multiple people from the same outside institution on the same project, but there appears to be a lack of civil servants involved in this one. The project’s “explicit reference to answering questions of interest to political appointees” is concerning, the employee says.
Boyd says this kind of work is a clear departure from the bureau’s mandate, which does not include providing data to political appointees. “These are all part of culture norms and practices of how you make certain you run a transparent agency to ensure that you are doing good by the American people,” she says.
There is precedent for political pressure at the Census Bureau: In 2021, less than two weeks after the January 6 insurrection at the end of Trump’s first term, then US Census Bureau director Steven Dillingham announced his resignation after a letter from the Office of the Inspector General revealed that whistleblowers had come forward to allege Census workers had been pressured by political appointees to create a report showing the citizenship status of every US resident.

articles.title: Uber expands options for riders with seniors accounts - Engadget
articles.text:
Uber expands options for riders with seniors accounts
The changes offer more independence and requests for easy vehicle entry.
Rideshare company Uber has announced changes aimed at riders who are senior citizens and those with limited mobility. The company said it is adding more options that allow for independence for its older riders. When the senior accounts first launched, they were intended for seniors who might want assistance from a family member with managing their rides. Senior accounts were required to be connected with a standard Uber account. Today's expansion adds a second option that allows a senior account to be set up and managed solo, without that family member for assistance.
No matter which of those choices an older rider takes, senior accounts now have a new settings page. It will allow them to set preferences including how a driver signals their arrival at pickup, a simple mode option with a more streamlined UI and an option to inform drivers of their notable identifiers such as use of a cane or walker.
Uber is also testing a new vehicle designation aimed at making rides more accessible both to seniors and to riders with limited mobility. During the pilot, a rider can opt to be assigned an Easy Entry Vehicle that doesn't require a high step to embark. Any Uber user can request Easy Entry Vehicle from the Accessibility settings page. The pilot phase will be running in nine markets, although Uber did not specify where those markets are.

articles.title: Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
articles.text:
You may not know it, but minivans are making a comeback in the US. Look around, and you’ll start to notice an uptick in these breadboxes on wheels. Sales were up 21 percent in 2025, suggesting that the humble minivan is shaking off its “uncool” stigma and finding new fans among an SUV-weary public. I’m here for it.
Kia’s electric van lineup is getting more interesting with reveal of PV7
The PV7 is longer than Kia’s previous electric van and comes in two versions: one for passengers and one for cargo.
One of the companies currently carrying the torch for minivans is Kia, which has sold its popular Carnival minivan here since 2021. Kia is also one of the few automakers making all-electric vans. This week, the Korean automaker rolled out its new PV7 at IAA Transportation in Germany. This is the second electric van from Kia’s Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) lineup, following the PV5 “people mover,” which went on sale in 2025. The PV7 is longer than the PV5 by about 2 feet and comes in two variants, one for passengers and one for cargo.
All of which is to say that Kia should bring its increasingly interesting electric vans to the US. If they are attractively priced — and this is Kia, so it’s safe to assume that’s possible — I really think these vans would do numbers. The people yearn for a moderately priced electric van!
The PBV vans are technically impressive on several levels. They’re built on Kia’s dedicated PBV architecture (E-GMP.S) that features a flat-floor layout for easy loading and unloading. The PV7 will come with a 71.5kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt battery pack or a 96.2kWh one. Kia claims the Cargo Long-Range version will get 460km (285.8 miles) on the generous WLTP cycle (which tends to be around 10–20 percent more generous than the EPA’s estimates). It’s built on an 800-volt architecture, which enables 10—80 percent charging in under 25 minutes using a 350kW DC fast charger. And it supports vehicle-to-load outlets to power external tools and equipment. The infotainment runs on Kia’s Android Automotive-based Pleos Connect OS, which includes its Gleo AI natural-language voice controls.
This all sounds great! And the design is just forward-looking enough to erase any concerns about the typical clunkiness of van ownership. The front end features a distinctive two-tone design with a dark upper section that wraps around the windshield, giving it a visor-like appearance. The upright look and tall, flat roof suggests a large interior space perfect for vanlife compartmentalization. The low front bumper and plastic body cladding around the base add a rugged, practical border. Both the passenger and cargo versions feature distinctive wheels with a squarish multi-spoke design. It’s not boring, but it’s not so in your face as to challenge your worldview.
While Kia’s not saying whether the PV7 will be making its way to the US anytime soon, a version has been spotted testing in the US, according to Electrek. Officially, the van will be launched in Europe and Korea in the second half of 2027, with “additional markets, derivatives and conversion models to follow.”
PBV was introduced during CES 2024 as a family of EVs built on a flexible vehicle architecture with different swappable body types. The vehicle can be transformed from a minivan to a full-size van to a small truck, depending on the specific need. The driver cab remains fixed, while the rest of the vehicle is interchangeable, like a real-life Duplo set. Of course, that was a concept from a different era. We’ve now veered into a darker timeline, at least for EVs.
I get why Kia would hesitate to name the US as a future market, what with our well-documented history of cutting off our nose to spite our face. The minivan market may not be as red-hot as, say, the one for lifted trucks that roll coal and grind up spandex-wearing cyclists for breakfast. But the times, they are a-changing. Gas prices are going up and up. And an electric van could just be thing that finally heals our broken nation.

articles.title: Wonder scores a $425 million partnership with DoorDash as it builds its food empire | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The delivery platform DoorDash is investing in and partnering with Marc Lore-owned food tech company Wonder in deals worth a total of $425 million, the company announced on Tuesday. DoorDash will acquire Wonder’s Grubhub Campus Dining business (formerly Tapingo) for $300 million and will add $125 million to Wonder’s $650 million Series D round, announced in July.
A chain of ghost kitchen food halls designed for delivery, Wonder is trying to take a one-size-fits-all approach to fast casual dining, allowing customers to order food from a variety of different restaurants, all under the same roof. Wonder, founded by veteran e-commerce entrepreneur Marc Lore, whose prior companies were acquired by Amazon and Walmart, is slowly building a takeout empire.
Last year, Wonder acquired the food delivery platform Grubhub for $650 million, adding to its portfolio of brands like Blue Apron and Tastemade. Wonder also bought the New York City-based restaurant chains Mighty Quinn’s BBQ, Salt Hank’s, and Blue Ribbon Fried Chicken.
Lore said in a statement that the DoorDash partnership allows Wonder to “focus on [its] long-term ambition: a fully autonomous food system that can plan, produce and deliver personalized meals at scale, serving all 21 meals people eat each week.”
With its acquisition, DoorDash said that it wants to expand Wonder’s Grubhub Campus Dining business, which is live at 450 colleges and universities, to stadiums, hotels, and other venues.
“Adding Grubhub Campus Dining to our platform will enable us to bring greater choice and convenience to college students while streamlining operations and reducing friction for universities,” DoorDash co-founder Tony Xu said in a statement.
For those who live in the Northeast or Mid-Atlantic regions, the fast growth of Wonder is palpable. It seems as though new stores are popping up all over the place, and it’s not an illusion. Wonder says it now has 157 locations, more than quadrupling its footprint since the start of 2025. It plans to expand to Texas in early 2027.

articles.title: BMW will show navigation and driver assistance in one 3D view from October
articles.text:
BMW will merge navigation and driver assistance into a single 3D view from October, on cars running its Operating System X, and says it will begin navigation-guided semi-automated urban driving in Germany in 2027. The UN regulation covering these systems only extends to system-initiated manoeuvres on urban roads from its 02 series, expected in force in late January 2027.
BMW will merge navigation and driver assistance into a single 3D view from October, the company said. It goes to cars running its Operating System X, which arrived with the new iX3.
The display puts the car in its lane and at the right road level, shows the surrounding traffic, and overlays what the assistance systems are doing. Stephan Durach, a BMW senior vice president, called the interaction between navigation and driver assistance “an important step toward highly automated driving“.
BMW built it in-house on mapping data from Mapbox, combining map data, vehicle sensors and artificial intelligence. The feature only works alongside Highway Assistant or Highway and City Assistant, in select countries, cities and roads, and rolls out in phases.
Tesla has drawn the car in its lane for years, so the look will be familiar to Model 3 drivers.
The interesting part is why BMW needs it now.
From 2027 BMW models with Operating System X will begin rolling out navigation-guided semi-automated driving in urban areas, initially in Germany. Today its Highway Assistant 2 runs hands-free on motorways to 130 kph, changing lane once the driver confirms with a glance.
That date is not arbitrary. These systems are governed by UN Regulation 171, and what a car may do without the driver steering depends on which series of it applies.
The first version took effect on 22 September 2024. The 01 series has been in force since 26 September 2025, permitting system-initiated manoeuvres on motorways and tightening the monitoring of hands and eyes.
The 02 series was adopted in June and is expected to take effect in late January 2027. It extends system-initiated manoeuvres to urban roads and widens the conditions for hands-off driving.
BMW was the first carmaker in Germany approved under the regulation, in late October 2025, covering the Motorway Assistant’s hands-off function and Active Lane Change with eye activation. That gives it a basis to offer those functions across many more European countries.
Tesla took the other route. The Netherlands cleared FSD Supervised under the 01 series using exemptions, because its urban behaviour goes beyond what that series allows.
BMW is waiting for the rule instead of asking for an exception. That is slower, and much harder for a regulator to reverse later.
Six more countries have since cleared Tesla’s system, and a bloc-wide vote is coming. The screen arriving in October is BMW’s answer to the same question.

articles.title: Lawmakers Want States to Crack Down on Flock Cameras—or Pay the Price
articles.text:
A bipartisan pair of US lawmakers tell WIRED they plan to introduce legislation today that would strip federal funding from states that fail to restrict the use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers. The devices, which help police track the location of vehicles tied to crimes, have become the subject of nationwide backlash in recent months over more nefarious uses by officers.
The No FLOCK Act—for Federal License-Plate Observation and Camera Keeping—directs the US secretary of transportation to withhold 10 percent of annual financial support due to states for highways, roads, and bridges if it fails to ban Flock and similar devices for all but five use cases. Congressmen Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democrat representing Chicago suburbs, and Michael Cloud, a Republican whose Texas district includes Corpus Christi, are cosponsoring the bill.
The legislation says that Flock cameras could be used only for “enforcing toll systems, identifying stolen vehicles, missing or endangered persons, vehicles registered to persons with a warrant for a felony offense, or investigating a vehicle involved in a felony offense.” Notably absent are uses like conducting traffic studies, investigating minor drug crimes, and enforcing parking and speeding rules.
“Our investigation into Flock exposed serious gaps in oversight, and this bipartisan bill would put clear limits in place to prevent abuse while preserving legitimate public safety uses,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement.
But the bill stops short of banning Flock systems altogether, which has been the number one demand from supporters of a global protest movement against the Atlanta-based company and its competitors. It also doesn’t stop Flock users from broadly sharing license plate tracking data with other government agencies, including immigration authorities.
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the proposed bill.
If the legislation is passes this year, states that fail to comply with it would begin losing out on tens of millions to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual transportation funding starting in October 2028.
The Department of Transportation calculates the amount of so-called surface transportation funds it gives to states based on factors such as how many roadways they have and how busy they are. Congress has repeatedly threatened taking away the funding to pressure states into taking action on public safety. The tactic helped establish a national minimum drinking age, standard rules for what constitutes driving under the influence, and regulations for billboards alongside highways.
Another bipartisan bill introduced in Congress recently called for banning the use of federal funding to purchase Flock cameras. Flock’s lobbying spending in Washington, DC, has been steady over the past 18 months, and it recently hired a fifth firm to help with the efforts, according to federal records.
Tech Backlash
A number of issues related to emerging technologies, including rogue AI systems, data center construction, and law enforcement abuse of Flock cameras, have become major topics in the upcoming US midterm elections, which are now less than two months away. But it’s unclear whether any legislation designed to address voters’ concerns will advance through Congress anytime soon, let alone gain the approval of President Donald Trump.
The president expressed support for Flock cameras on Sunday, telling reporters that they help law enforcement authorities. Lawmakers largely agree, but they are frustrated by cases in which police officers have been caught using Flock footage for personal reasons, such as stalking their one-time romantic partners. One report found at least 100 instances of alleged abuse over the past eight years.
“Taxpayers shouldn't be forced to fund the shredding of their own civil liberties or the growth of a surveillance state,” Cloud said in a statement. “Flock cameras are enabling mass surveillance of Americans, infringing on the Fourth Amendment.”
About 25 states and US territories have laws about automated license plate readers, including mandating transparency about the systems and requiring unnecessary data to be promptly deleted, but few of the measures limit types of uses, according to the New York University School of Law’s Policing Project.
The bill is “a first step toward reining in unchecked surveillance,” Cloud said, adding, “we can protect public safety without sacrificing the privacy of Americans.”
