articles.title: Thu nhập 25 triệu, mỗi tháng mất 6,5 triệu trả góp đồ gia dụng
articles.text:
Mới ra trường, chưa có thu nhập ổn định, Trúc Quỳnh (25 tuổi, Hà Nội) quyết định mua smartphone mới giá 20 triệu đồng bằng hình thức trả góp hàng tháng. Quỳnh phải trả trước 5 triệu đồng, phần còn lại 15 triệu đồng được chia trong 12 tháng, tương đương 1,25 triệu đồng mỗi tháng.
Ngoài ra, Quỳnh phải trả thêm 300.000 đồng phí hồ sơ và 50.000 đồng phí dịch vụ mỗi tháng trong 12 tháng. Như vậy, tổng số tiền phải trả cho chiếc điện thoại là 20,9 triệu đồng.
Quỳnh tiếp tục mua một số món đồ công nghệ và quần áo bằng hình thức mua trước, trả sau. Do mỗi khoản thanh toán được chia nhỏ, cô không cảm thấy áp lực tại thời điểm mua.
“Từng khoản không quá lớn nên tôi nghĩ vẫn có thể cân đối được. Nhưng khi cộng lại, mỗi tháng tôi phải dành một khoản đáng kể chỉ để trả những món đã mua từ trước”, Quỳnh cho biết.
Điều khiến cô bắt đầu chú ý là số tiền phải thanh toán cố định mỗi tháng ngày càng tăng, trong khi mức lương không thay đổi. Ngoài ra, Quỳnh còn phải trả tiền thuê nhà, ăn uống, đi lại và chi phí sinh hoạt khác.
Tương tự, vợ chồng anh Hùng (Ninh Bình) sắm thiết bị gia dụng theo hình thức này. Sau khi xây nhà, phần lớn tiền tiết kiệm đã được sử dụng nên hai vợ chồng chọn mua trả góp một số thiết bị.
Chiếc tivi giá 15 triệu đồng được trả trong 12 tháng, tương đương 1,25 triệu đồng/tháng. Chiếc tủ lạnh giá 15 triệu đồng cũng được trả trong 12 tháng, thêm 1,25 triệu đồng mỗi tháng. Máy giặt giá 12 triệu đồng tương đương 1 triệu đồng/tháng. Điều hòa cho các phòng có tổng giá trị 36 triệu đồng, tương đương 3 triệu đồng/tháng nếu chia trong 12 tháng.
Chỉ riêng 4 thiết bị này, gia đình Hùng phải dành khoảng 6,5 triệu đồng/tháng để trả góp.
Với thu nhập của hai vợ chồng là 25 triệu đồng/tháng, riêng các khoản trả góp này đã chiếm 26% thu nhập, tương đương hơn 1/4 tổng thu nhập của gia đình. Số tiền còn lại phải dùng để trang trải học phí cho con, ăn uống và các khoản phát sinh khác. Nếu thu nhập giảm hoặc phát sinh khoản chi bất ngờ, khoản trả góp cố định hàng tháng có thể làm gia đình khó xoay xở hơn về tài chính.
Đừng chỉ nhìn vào số tiền phải trả mỗi tháng
Theo ông Nguyễn Mạnh Cường, chuyên viên tư vấn tài chính, các chương trình trả góp 0% có thể giúp người mua giảm áp lực thanh toán ngay tại thời điểm mua hàng. Tuy nhiên, ngay cả khi không phát sinh lãi suất, người mua vẫn có thể chịu áp lực nếu đồng thời có nhiều nghĩa vụ thanh toán.
Một quyết định mua hàng tưởng như chỉ làm tăng chi tiêu 2 triệu đồng/tháng nhưng thực tế có thể khiến ngân sách trở nên căng thẳng hơn trong nhiều tháng liên tiếp.
Một nguyên tắc đơn giản là lập danh sách tất cả các khoản trả góp, ngày đến hạn và số tiền phải trả. Sau đó, cộng với các khoản chi cố định như tiền thuê nhà, điện nước, ăn uống, bảo hiểm và các khoản nợ khác.
Nếu sau khi trừ toàn bộ nghĩa vụ cố định mà số tiền còn lại quá thấp, việc mua thêm một món đồ trả góp có thể làm giảm đáng kể khoản tiền dành cho các chi tiêu thiết yếu.
Với những món đồ không thực sự cần thiết, người tiêu dùng có thể áp dụng nguyên tắc chờ một khoảng thời gian trước khi mua. Nếu sau thời gian đó vẫn thấy cần thiết và đã có sẵn nguồn tiền, quyết định mua sẽ ít tạo áp lực hơn.
Người mua cũng cần kiểm tra kỹ các khoản phí trước khi ký hợp đồng. Nếu chiếc điện thoại giá 30 triệu đồng có thêm phí hồ sơ hoặc phí dịch vụ, tổng số tiền thực tế phải trả sẽ cao hơn giá niêm yết.
Đặc biệt, người tiêu dùng nên tránh dùng một khoản vay hoặc hình thức trả sau mới để xử lý khoản thanh toán cũ. Việc liên tục kéo dài nghĩa vụ tài chính có thể khiến một khoản chi tiêu nhỏ trở thành áp lực lớn đối với ngân sách.
Trước khi bấm nút mua, người dùng nên trả lời ba câu hỏi: Tôi có thực sự cần món đồ này không? Tổng số tiền phải trả là bao nhiêu? Nếu thu nhập giảm trong một vài tháng, tôi có vẫn trả được đúng hạn không?

articles.title: India ends free ride for larger transactions on its ubiquitous digital payments network | TechCrunch
articles.text:
India has finally put a price on larger transactions on its ubiquitous digital payments network, ending years of free processing for merchants as authorities seek to make a system used for billions of payments each month financially self-sustaining.
The country’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI) will impose a 0.4% merchant fee on certain payments above ₹2,000 (about $21) from October 15, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which operates the network, said on Tuesday. Consumers will continue to use the service for free, NPCI said.
Credit card merchant fees typically range from 1.5% to 2.5% per transaction, while debit card fees are capped at 0.9%, according to an FAQ (PDF) released by NPCI.
UPI’s merchant fee is capped at ₹300 (about $3) for transactions of ₹75,000 (around $783) or more, while payments of ₹2,000 or less will remain free for merchants. Small merchants receiving up to ₹100,000 (about $1,041) a month through UPI will also be exempt from the charges.
Some sectors, including railways, telecom, insurance, and fuel, will pay a flat ₹5 (about 5 cents) fee on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. Capital-market transactions will attract a 0.02% fee, capped at ₹300, NPCI said.
The move marks a major shift for a payments system that has been free for merchants to accept since 2020. It has been long anticipated by the payments industry, which has argued that the zero-fee model made it difficult to cover the growing cost of operating the network.
In August, New Delhi laid the groundwork for the shift when it amended India’s payments law to allow merchant fees on some UPI transactions. A notification issued on Monday specified that banks cannot levy charges on UPI payments of up to ₹2,000, clearing the way for fees on larger transactions.
UPI has emerged as the spine of India’s digital payments economy, processing 24.51 billion transactions worth ₹29.9 trillion (about $312 billion) in August alone, per the recent data by NPCI. Its ubiquity over the last few years has made scanning a QR code one of the most common ways to pay in India.
India scrapped merchant fees on UPI payments in January 2020 to boost adoption. The Indian government has since subsidized banks and payment firms for processing some of those transactions.
However, authorities have argued for the last few months that the cost of operating UPI at such a vast scale makes the current model unsustainable. Industry estimates, per NPCI, put the annual cost of running the network, including server capacity, fraud prevention, and technical support, at about ₹200 billion ($2.1 billion).
The newly announced merchant fees, NPCI said, will be distributed among participants in the UPI ecosystem and used to fund investments in infrastructure, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, and customer service.
NPCI did not respond to questions about how it arrived at the ₹200 billion annual cost estimate, how much revenue it expects the new fees to generate, or how that revenue will be distributed across the UPI ecosystem.
The shift has raised questions over whether charging merchants could chip away at one of UPI’s biggest attractions: its cost. Even though consumers will not be charged directly, businesses accepting larger payments will now have to absorb a fee that did not exist before.
Krishnamurthy Subramanian, a former chief economic adviser to the Indian government, noted that UPI should be treated as digital public infrastructure whose benefits extend well beyond individual transactions, including by reducing reliance on cash, bringing more businesses into the formal economy, and widening access to digital payments.
“The right question is: what is the opportunity cost of charging UPI transactions and what are its social benefits?” Subramanian wrote in a post on X.
The debate also comes as India continues to bear the cost of maintaining a vast cash network. Currency in circulation is still growing at double-digit rates even as cash accounts for a declining share of individual transactions, as the BBC recently reported, citing data from the Reserve Bank of India.
NPCI has sought to limit that risk by keeping smaller transactions outside the new fee regime. Payments of up to ₹2,000 account for more than 95% of UPI merchant transactions by volume, it said.
The payments operator also plans to use part of the fees to create a fund aimed at expanding digital-payment infrastructure and merchant adoption in smaller cities and rural areas. The fund’s details will be worked out with India’s central bank over the next three months, NPCI said.
The new fee could also provide a revenue boost to payment companies that have spent heavily building the infrastructure to process UPI transactions. Fintech firms including Paytm and Pine Labs, as well as IPO-bound PhonePe and Razorpay, are among the companies that could benefit as the merchant fee is distributed across the payments ecosystem.
That said, the bigger test of the move will come once the fees take effect, and whether merchants absorb the added cost or encourage customers to use other payment methods, particularly for larger purchases and in businesses with thin margins.
Merchants will not be allowed to pass the fee on to customers, NPCI said, arguing that the 0.4% charge is low enough for businesses to absorb. Consumers will continue to pay the listed price regardless of whether they use UPI, it stated.

articles.title: Apple adds TV and Arcade to iCloud+ subscriptions in 100 countries - Engadget
articles.text:
Apple adds TV and Arcade to iCloud+ subscriptions in 100 countries
But the new iCloud+ bundle isn’t available in the US.
Apple is upgrading its iCloud+ subscriptions in select locations. iCloud+ already gives subscribers access to bigger storage, along with privacy and security features like Private Relay that hides IP addresses and Hide My Email, which the user can use to create random email addresses. Now, the company is also bundling Apple TV and Arcade with iCloud+ subscriptions in over 100 countries.
The company already sells several subscription products in a bundle called Apple One, which includes iCloud+, Apple TV, Music and Arcade. But for at least $20 a month, it's a lot more expensive than a standalone iCloud+ membership. The cheapest iCloud+ plan is only $1 in the US, and it costs pretty much the equivalent of that in local currencies in other regions.
With the inclusion of TV and Arcade in $1 iCloud+ subscriptions, it seems like Apple is no longer pushing its One bundle in certain locations. It's possible that the company has realized that its services could achieve more growth in those regions if it makes them more affordable and accessible. As 9to5Mac notes, the company is even bundling in Apple Music Select, which will give iCloud+ subscribers access to a handful of ad-free internet radio stations. It's also worth noting that this rollout will expand Apple TV's availability to 59 new countries.
Unfortunately, the new iCloud+ bundle isn't available in the United States. You can find all the regions where it's available below, but they include India, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: A New Headset to Help With Depression Is Now Available in the US
articles.text:
An at-home wearable for the treatment of depression is now available by prescription in the US.
With roughly one in six American adults taking an antidepressant medication, Swedish firm Flow Neuroscience is positioning its device as an alternative to traditional drugs. But at the current four-figure price tag, it might take a while for the futuristic-looking headset to catch on with patients.
Worn on the forehead for 30 minutes a day and operated with an app, the device provides low-intensity electrical stimulation to the left frontal lobe of the brain, an area involved in regulating mood and emotions. People with depression tend to have lower activity and weaker neural connections in that part of the brain.
Flow received approval from the Food and Drug Administration last December, and its device is among a new breed of wearables that monitor, record from, or stimulate the brain. California-based Cognixion, for instance, has modified the Apple Vision Pro to build a communication system for paralyzed people that doesn’t depend on speech or motor control. A headband by Muse promises to improve meditation, and a device by Elemind is meant to help people fall asleep faster.
The Flow device targets the same part of the brain as transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, an approved treatment for depression that uses magnetic fields to activate neurons. With TMS, patients have to go to a clinic, and a full dosing series typically requires treatment sessions administered five days a week over several weeks. The whole course of treatment can cost up to $15,000 without insurance.
Flow CEO Daniel Månsson, a clinical psychologist before he cofounded the company, says he set out to make a more convenient option for patients. “In order to have a real impact on the problem, you need to create something that has the effect on the brain needed, but that can be used in a home environment in a safe and effective way,” he says.
In a trial of 174 people with major depressive disorder, 45 percent of participants who received Flow’s device experienced a remission in symptoms at 10 weeks compared to 22 percent of those in a control group who received a sham version. The trial included people who were taking antidepressants and those who weren’t—evidence that the device can, under medical supervision, be used in addition to medication, Månsson says.
Reported side effects were mild: Some people experienced skin irritation, headaches, and trouble concentrating. Antidepressants, meanwhile, can cause nausea, weight gain, drowsiness, dry mouth, and sexual problems, but these can go away a few weeks after beginning medication.
In Europe, where the device has been approved since 2019, more than 65,000 people have used the Flow device, says Månsson. The UK’s National Health Service is also piloting the headset.
In the US, patients will be able to get a prescription for the Flow device from a clinician in person or via telehealth. But at least for now, they’ll have to pay out of pocket to use it: $2,200 for 10 weeks and then $325 per month after. That’s a lot more than standard antidepressants, which are usually covered by insurance. Månsson says the company is working to get reimbursement from insurers.
Vinod Khosla, a billionaire venture capitalist and an early investor in Flow, thinks a nonchemical approach to treating depression is the way of the future. “My bet is, if you ask any person who's on depression drugs, they'd prefer not to be on them,” he says. “They'd like a nondrug, nonchemical treatment for it.”

articles.title: Vintage Violence is an absurdist crime thriller for phone addicts
articles.text:
There are a lot of movies that have tried to seamlessly integrate modern tech — text messages, livestreams, etc. — into their storytelling. Some of the most novel attempts have been in the genre space, like the Twitch-style horror flick Deadstream. But the most chaotic to date might just be Vintage Violence, an absurd crime thriller with lots of blood, jokes, and screentime.
Vintage Violence is an absurdist crime thriller for phone addicts
Reviews from TIFF 2026: Vintage Violence, Ken Russell’s The Devils in 4K, and Gentle Monster.
I was able to catch Vintage Violence, the latest from director Eugene Kotlyarenko, on my fifth day at the Toronto International Film Festival. Kotlyarenko has previously explored our hyper-connected culture in 2020’s Spree, a movie in which Stranger Things’ Joe Keery plays a rideshare driver who starts murdering passengers while livestreaming the crimes. But Vintage Violence takes things a step further by trying to replicate what it’s like to constantly be on your phone as the movie plays out. It’s a lot to take in, but I really enjoyed it. Unfortunately there isn’t a trailer yet to give you a better sense of how things work onscreen, but I’ll make sure to share it when they do release one.
Vintage Violence was one of three films I took in on day 5 of TIFF 2026; the others were a 4K restoration of a cult classic and a devastating drama that’s on its way to Netflix. Here are my thoughts on all three.
Vintage Violence
No theatrical date yet
From the premise alone you can tell this movie is ridiculous. Carter (Cole Sprouse), a disgraced MrBeast-style influencer, finds a cache of vintage Levi’s while livestreaming, and one of his fans, Izumi (Kiko Mizuhara), suggests he comes to Tokyo to sell the denim for some big cash. When he gets there, just about everyone is running some kind of scam — pretty quickly the yakuza get involved, including an enforcer with a prosthetic middle finger — and things play out like a toned-down, but still brutal and bloody, Takashi Miike film. But what really elevates Vintage Violence is the way it constantly displays what characters are doing on their phones right alongside the main film. That means everything from sending text messages to livestreaming to listening to whale sounds to relax. It can get chaotic and a challenge to follow — at one point I was trying to read the chat on a Kick stream while an action scene played out beside it — but that’s also kind of the point.
Ken Russell’s The Devils
In theaters on October 16th
The Devils is one of those cult classics I’ve always meant to watch but never got around to. But this new 4K theatrical rerelease was the perfect excuse. First released in 1971, The Devils is a surreal and disturbing account of a witch trial in a small, independent town in 17th-century France. Run by an impossibly handsome priest (Oliver Reed) who openly defies a powerful cardinal, the town soon descends into pure hysteria following reports of demonic possession, which the church seizes on in order to oust the priest. This version is not only a remaster but also a director’s cut — it’s rated NC-17 — and while I can’t speak to what’s new since I hadn’t seen it before, I will say the film rarely shows its age, with enthralling and disturbing sequences merged with a poignant story about the dangers of mixing politics and religion. And in 4K the stark architecture and uncomfortable violence really pop on the big screen.
Gentle Monster
In theaters on October 30th; streaming on Netflix on November 18th
Marie Kreutzer’s latest feature is a difficult watch. It follows a young family that is torn apart when the police arrive at their country home one day to seize the father’s digital devices as part of a CSAM investigation. The story is primarily centered on the mother, Lucy (Léa Seydoux), a pianist who struggles with accepting a truth that threatens to upend her entire world. Gentle Monster does a remarkable job of slowly taking you through Lucy’s complicated, messy, and constantly changing understanding of the situation, but what really makes it work is Seydoux’s raw and unnerving performance, which oscillates between wishing the problem would go away to doing anything she can to protect her son. It’s a great film, but one that’s certain to leave you unsettled.

articles.title: Hate Mac and Windows? This Is the Best Linux Laptop Around
articles.text:
I have similar feelings about the very large glass trackpad. For things like photo editing, the trackpad's size is great, but I found my palms occasionally clicked the buttons at the bottom of the trackpad when I took a break from typing. It didn't happen often, but I learned to be careful about where I put my palms.
The 2-MP 1080p webcam is fine for casual use, chatting with family and friends, but if you do a lot of Zoom meetings in a professional context, you may want an external webcam. Also, open-source purists should note that Coreboot still does not support AMD Ryzen chips (or AMD does not support Coreboot, depending on how you want to look at it), so the Pangolin Pro does not use open firmware.
Finally, the Pangolin Pro is easy to open up to replace or repair components. There are nine screws on the bottom of the chassis, and none of them are hidden under the rubber feet or other shenanigans. Unscrew them all, and the bottom lifts off, giving you access to the SSD slots, RAM, WiFi card, and the rest of the internals. You'll have no trouble upgrading components down the road if you decide to, say, upgrade your memory when RAM prices come back down. (Is that actually going to happen? Who knows.)
Pop!_OS Linux Integration
System76's Pop!_OS Linux has long provided what I consider one of the best Linux experiences out there. The Cosmic Desktop and the custom apps System76 ships with it provide that "just works" stability you need to use Linux daily without even noticing you're using Linux.
As a long-time Linux user, I'm probably biased, but I find Linux to offer a better user experience than MacOS or Windows. I never feel like I'm fighting the operating system to get things the way I want them. I mainly run a terminal for writing, email, reading RSS feeds, etc, and a web browser. When I need to edit photos, I open Darktable; videos in DaVinci Resolve. None of that should require much from an operating system, but for some reason it's all easier for me in Linux.
Pop!_OS is particularly good in this regard, as it manages to feel familiar enough for Linux newcomers to find their way around, while still offering a good amount of power-user features. For instance, if you don't know what tiling windows are, you never need to be bothered about them, but if you want them, you can enable them with a toggle switch in the settings app. There are loads of (customizable) keyboard shortcuts for developers who eschew the mouse, and there are plenty of trackpad gestures to control workspaces, window focus, and more.
Should You Buy It?
At the beginning, I said the Pangolin Pro is overkill for most peoples needs, which is true. Although the Pangolin is actually cheaper than the smaller System76 Lemur Pro (review coming soon), the more portable Lemur Pro might be a better fit for many. However, if you're doing highly intensive things with your laptop, building local AI models or training custom agents, compiling software, or just want a powerful, future-proof machine, Pangolin is one of the best Linux laptops I've tested.
If you're a Linux user looking for a 16-inch laptop with all the bells and whistles, and one that isn't crazy expensive or crazy heavy, this is the machine I would get.

articles.title: Lidl and Einride put a driverless truck into daily service in Germany
articles.text:
Lidl has put Einride’s cab-less Level 4 electric truck into daily service between a logistics centre and a store in Germany, under a first-of-its-kind permit from the federal transport authority. The route appears to be less than a mile, and the permit is national, so it does not travel across European borders.
Lidl has put a cab-less autonomous truck into daily service on German public roads, Einride said. It is the country’s first Level 4 truck built without a cab to run in commercial operations.
Einride built it, and the federal transport authority granted a first-of-its-kind permit. The Swedish company already rents about 200 electric trucks to customers including Heineken and PepsiCo.
There is no driver and no safety monitor on board. A remote operator watches, and can move the vehicle at up to 6 kph to handle docking and edge cases, but does not drive it.
The truck carries nine cameras, six radars and four lidars, and is assembled by a contract manufacturer in the Netherlands.
It runs one shift a day, five days a week, carrying about 45 pallets between a distribution centre and a store at Edermunde in Hesse. Lidl’s head of operational logistics in Germany, Thomas Dangelmayer, described it as a milestone being tested step by step in real operations.
The route is very short.
Comparing the footage against Street View, InsideEVs put the distance at under a mile, with the store sitting next to the warehouse. Einride says the next step is a milkrun with several stops.
The permit is the achievement here, not the mileage. Einride’s chief executive Roozbeh Charli called German clearance “among the toughest in the world“.
Germany rewrote its Road Traffic Act in 2021 and followed it with an ordinance that lets a driverless Level 4 vehicle operate inside a defined operational area, approved case by case.
No other European country has an equivalent national route carrying goods every day, and Berlin is treating it as a showcase. A transport ministry state secretary, Christian Hirte, said projects like this establish Germany as a pioneer in deploying advanced mobility technology.
That is also the limit. EU type approval for automated driving systems exists under a 2022 regulation, but the permission to operate stays with each member state, which is why Waymo is starting in Munich rather than anywhere else.
Einride would have to win this argument again in every country it enters. It is already in talks with Lidl’s parent about putting more trucks on the road.
The company listed on Nasdaq in June at a $1.35B valuation, down from the $5B it once discussed with banks. A permit nobody else in Europe holds is worth more to it than a mile of road.

articles.title: Apple TV cleaned up at the Emmys with eight wins for Widow's Bay and Pluribus - Engadget
articles.text:
Apple TV cleaned up at the Emmys with eight wins for Widow's Bay and Pluribus
Matthew Rhys made history as the first lead actor to win the same award in two different categories.
Apple TV has only been around for seven years but it just beat 55-year-old HBO for the prestige TV crown in 2026 (again). Apple's streaming service collected eight Primetime Emmy awards last night, including six for Widow's Bay and two for Pluribus. That's on top of the 20 Creative Arts Emmys it won earlier, bringing the platform's total to 28 in 2026. HBO, meanwhile, won five Primetime Emmys this year (plus 16 Creative Arts Emmys), while Netflix took home three, along with 13 Creative Arts Emmys.
After earning 19 nominations, comedy horror Widow's Bay was Apple TV's big winner this year. It garnered Emmys for best comedy series, lead actor in a comedy series (Matthew Rhys), supporting actor and actress in a comedy series (Stephen Root and Kate O'Flynn), outstanding writing for a comedy series (Katie Dipold) and outstanding directing for a comedy series (Hiro Murai). Critical darling Pluribus picked up two awards for lead actress in a drama series (Rhea Seehorn) and outstanding writing for a drama series (Vince Gilligan).
HBO's big winners were The Pitt and Hacks, a drama and comedy about emergency medicine and comedy, respectively. The Pitt won for drama series and lead actor (Noah Wyle), two of the more prestigious prizes of the night. Jean Smart took home the lead actress in a comedy series award for Hacks, while DTF St Louis took the Emmy for best limited or anthology series and Tom Pelphrey won best supporting actor in a drama series for Task.
Finally, Netflix won Allison Janney an Emmy for best supporting actress in The Diplomat, while Sally Field really, really liked winning lead actress in a limited or anthology series for Remarkably Bright Creatures. Finally, Matthew Rhys took home a second lead acting award (limited or anthology series) for Netflix's The Beast in Me — the first time that's ever happened at the Primetime Emmys.

articles.title: Now Light’s minimalist phone can easily call an Uber
articles.text:
More than a decade after its Kickstarter proposed a “cell phone designed to be used as little as possible,” Light is adding a direct connection to Uber and Lyft with a new Rideshare tool. For owners of either the Light Phone III or the upcoming Light Flip, they can use it to find pick up / drop off locations, see fares and ETA, and select different trip options or saved locations they frequently visit. They can use it to book the ride, and then see information about the driver and ETA, and call the driver if necessary.
Now Light’s minimalist phone can easily call an Uber
The monochrome Light phones are adding access to rideshare services while still minimizing feeds and notifications.
It’s an early preview of the LightOS “tool library” SDK that will allow developers to expand the phones’ features while still promising to minimize feeds and notifications. A blog post from Light says that “We’ll open up user submissions for the Tool Library by the end of this month, and look forward to having those available to everyone a few weeks after that!”
The rideshare integration works via a partnership with Tremp, which already operates an SMS-based way to order rideshares, and users set up access via Light’s dashboard website, just like other LightOS tools. It’s not free to use, however, as Tremp charges a 10 percent service fee with a $2 minimum, but it will waive that fee for the first five rides within 30 days of creating an account.
The pictures show all the necessary features operating, although we will have to see it in operation to find out if there are any hang-ups. The expansion of app-like features on a minimalist smartphone might seem counterintuitive, but Light cofounder Kaiwei Tang has addressed that previously, saying, “I’m not trying to design vintage phones… I want to design all this modern technology, from the ground up, and eliminate all the bullshit.”
That’s why adding one feature users absolutely need access to — whether it’s a way to call for a ride, access to Spotify playlists, or something else — might be a way to keep them from swapping back to another device with more algorithms and alerts that constantly pop up.

articles.title: Evvy raises $40M as it seeks to further women's health research with vaginal microbiome data | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Women’s health company Evvy on Tuesday said it has raised a $40 million Series B led by Catalio Capital Management.
Launched in 2021 by Priyanka Jain, Laine Bruzek, and Pita Navarro, the company is best known for operating what it touts as the world’s only at-home CLIA-certified and CLEP-certified mNGS test to analyze vaginal microbes with one swab.
The user mails their swab samples to Evvy’s lab, which then analyzes the results using its own mNGS sequencing, sends them to clinicians registered on its platform for review, and posts the results online in the patient’s health portal.
“When a patient receives their results, they are presented alongside a diagnosis, clinical interpretation, and a clear path of next steps, including personalized prescription care when relevant,” CEO and co-founder Priyanka Jain told TechCrunch.
Since its launch, Evvy says it now serves more than 100,000 patients across the United States, and works with 3,000 practitioners. “We’ve generated 15 peer-reviewed publications and abstracts, identified novel BV subtypes, and discovered hundreds of previously uncatalogued vaginal microbiome genomes,” Jain said.
She added that clinicians on Evvy can now leverage the collected data to offer personalized treatment to patients.
But treating patients is only one part of the company’s vision. Its bigger goal is to build a dataset that connects microbiome biology, symptoms, interventions, and health outcomes, “creating a continuous feedback loop that unlocks improvements to care and the discovery of entirely new biomarkers,” Jain said.
There is a fundamental flaw right now with precision medicine: the lack of high-quality, representative data on female bodies. “You can’t build precision medicine for women on datasets that never adequately measured female biology in the first place,” Jain said, citing how leading AI models often struggle to answer questions about women’s health.
“That’s why I believe AI for women’s health needs to be paired with new biological data at scale. AI can help us identify patterns across molecular signals, hormones, symptoms, treatments, fertility outcomes, and other biomarkers that traditional medicine has struggled to connect.”
In May, the company started offering its own AI assistant called EvvyAI, which it bills as an advisor for vaginal health. It translates the microbiome data that Evvy has collected into real-time guidance for users, and directs patients to clinicians for questions that need expert opinions.
When Evvy launched, Jain said it was with the belief that she and the team could leverage certain indicators in the vaginal biome to “predict and improve outcomes across the female lifespan,” she said. With that in mind, the startup is also now entering the fertility space, its first major foray beyond vaginal health.
Right now, the company is still compiling data and science, specifically linking vaginal microbiomes to infertility, gynecological cancer, preterm birth, IVF success rates, and recurrent pregnancy loss. The company last year launched a prospective study leveraging its vaginal microbiome tests in IVF clinics.
Hopefully, Jain said, collecting more data in women’s health can help the industry move away from the unexplained. “Women shouldn’t have to accept unexplained infertility, unexplained recurrence, or unexplained symptoms as answers when what they often mean is that medicine hasn’t caught up to the data yet.”
But things are improving. Besides Evvy, others in the vaginal health space include Juno Bio, Tiny Health, and Daye.
In the long term, Jain hopes that Evvy can create a new-age Pap smear. “An at-home, non-invasive sample that can provide women with more regular, data-rich insights across infections, inflammation, fertility, PCOC, endometriosis, premenopause, HPV progression, and more,” she said.
“I don’t think we can wait for traditional research methods to catch up,” she said. “I believe women, as patients, can be part of pushing the industry forward.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s Jack Clark: AI kill switches may need rules
articles.text:
Jack Clark says lawmakers may need to make AI “kill switches” mandatory. Clark is a co-founder of Anthropic and its head of policy. He told the BBC that outside parties should perhaps be able to check those switches too, in an interview published on 14 September.
Economics editor Faisal Islam asked whether Anthropic could pull the plug on its systems. Clark said most labs have ways to do that, and that Anthropic has systems in place. He added that the question belongs in the wider policy debate.
“Should you mandate that companies definitely have a kill switch and is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?” he asked. Society “might want to eventually pass rules around” that, he said.
What Clark says has changed
Clark said AI risks that were once theoretical are now showing up in real systems. AI agents are programs that run for long periods on set goals. This summer, he said, agents coordinated with each other and sometimes acted against their instructions. In some cases they hacked out of one company and into others.
Last year, Anthropic researchers showed agents lying or trying to escape test environments in simulations. This year, Clark said, the same kind of behaviour has appeared in real systems.
Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger has put the chance of human extinction from AI at more than 10%. He did so after researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company. Clark said he did not share that figure and that such statistics were not that useful.
He still warned against leaving AI as a largely unregulated industry. “We are rolling dice with immense risks,” he said. He added that it was not too late to act. In his view, the industry has not yet reached the most dangerous stage.
Third-party testers inside Anthropic
Over the weekend, chief executive Dario Amodei called for the industry to slow down in an essay. Clark described three steps from it. The first is outside auditors inside AI companies. The second is common safety standards that industry agrees and governments back. The third is dialogue between the great powers, including the US and China.
Anthropic has already agreed to bring third-party evaluators into its lab within weeks, Clark said. He named METR as one of the testing groups. He said the move would cause some friction inside the company.
Clark said Anthropic was at first the only company to back California’s SB 53 transparency law. It was also the only one backing New York’s RAISE Act until others joined, he said. Anthropic is now proposing a US framework that would make some safety tests mandatory.
He compared the idea to safety rules for baby toys, cars, and planes. Any country could set standards that AI products must pass before sale, he said.
Trump, China, and jobs
President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow AI down. He wrote on Truth Social that AI only needs a strong and smart president as its guardrail. He later called AI safety fears a “HOAX,” the BBC reported.
Clark said Anthropic was grateful that the president was paying attention to the issue. He argued that countries lose their lead in a technology when an accident destroys public trust. He gave nuclear power as an example.
China has criticised the slowdown push. Clark said Chinese models were six months to a year behind the West. China would face the same risks within months, he said. He added that the goal of the proposals was safety, not blocking competitors.
Clark said he leads a team of economists at Anthropic, which has built a new economic model. In that model, a large jump in AI capabilities brings a big rise in GDP. It also brings unprecedented white-collar unemployment. Clark called that jump the default path if governments do not act.
Kill switch proposals elsewhere
In the US, lawmakers have proposed a bill called the Kill Switch Act, the BBC reported. The bill would make companies keep a means of turning off AI tools that cause problems. Some government agencies would also gain powers to order those tools shut down or restricted.
The UK government has rejected the idea. A spokesperson told the BBC that a kill switch “would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere.”
Other industry leaders have backed parts of Anthropic’s call. OpenAI’s Sam Altman said OpenAI would also slow down. Clark said Elon Musk and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis had also spoken positively about the proposals.

articles.title: Meta’s new One subscriptions put a price on social media and AI
articles.text:
Shortly after launching its new do-everything AI assistant Muse, Meta’s launching subscription bundles that pair its standalone app subscriptions with extra AI usage. Some of the new Meta One bundles were in testing earlier this year, but are now available globally starting today, with several tiers for individual users, creators, and businesses. Meta says the “core experience” on its apps and Meta AI will still be free, and users can still get its subscriptions for Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp without a bundle. It also says it plans to expand the bundles to include “Edits, AI glasses, and more over time.”
Meta’s new One subscriptions put a price on social media and AI
Meta One bundles start at $7.99 per month with perks like 48-hour Instagram stories and a bold follow button.
There are two bundles for individual users, Core for $7.99 per month and Premium for $19.99 per month. They include Instagram Plus, WhatsApp Plus, and Facebook Plus, with “more media generation with Meta AI,” like generating images with Muse or using in-app AI features like Instagram’s Restyle. That’s a few dollars cheaper than paying $11 per month for all three of the standalone subscriptions.
The Meta One subscriptions aimed at creators and businesses range from $14.99 to $499 per month. They also include Meta’s individual app subscriptions, along with perks like a bold follow button, a verified badge, higher rankings in search results, and monitoring for fake impersonation accounts:
- Essential ($14.99/month): Establish yourself and build confidence with new audiences. Get tools to manage your presence and more access to Meta Business Agent on WhatsApp to respond to customers 24/7. Plus, a verified badge, verified channel on WhatsApp Business app, and impersonation protection so people know you’re who you say you are (pending successful verification).
- Advanced ($49.99/month): Invest in professional-grade tools. Advanced publishing features like scheduling stories up to 30 days in advance, links in organic posts and reels, exportable analytics, and deeper audience insights. Give team members access to your account without sharing your password and get more linked devices and business broadcast credits on WhatsApp. Plus, even more Meta Business Agent responses.
- Expert ($149/month) and Max ($499/month): Scale and optimize. These plans include our highest levels of feature access and Meta Business Agent capacity for teams managing at scale.

articles.title: 2028 Volvo XC60 and XC90 first look: Double the range and smarter safety, too - Engadget
articles.text:
2028 Volvo XC60 and XC90 first look: Double the range and smarter safety, too
Volvo caters to EV-curious buyers with way more range in its plug-in hybrid SUVs.
Given the current uncertainty in the global economy, you can forgive companies for hedging their bets and trying to cover as many bases as possible. In the automotive industry, that means leaning heavier than ever into hybrids that bridge the gap between the practicalities of internal combustion and the benefits of electrification.
With the upcoming versions of its XC60 and XC90 SUVs, Volvo is certainly aiming for the middle ground by delivering big upgrades to its plug-in hybrids. How big? More than doubling their all-electric range and, in the case of the XC60, creating a two-row, five-passenger SUV that can go 78 miles emissions-free and 590 miles total on a full charge and full tank of gas.
Familiar engine, new battery
That extra range comes courtesy of a revised powertrain that relies on the same 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine combined with electric motors as previous models, but it's now paired with an even bigger battery pack in the middle. Specifically, it offers 41.2-kilowatt-hours of capacity, of which 37.9 kWh is usable.
The result is unchanged system power output, specifically 455 horsepower through all four wheels, but you get that boosted 78-mile range figure. That's way up from the 35 miles on a charge before.
The bigger, three-row XC90 gets the same powertrain upgrade, running the same engine-and-motor combination to deliver 73 miles on a charge and 560 miles of total range if you factor in a tank of gasoline, too.
That extra all-electric range should make these machines a lot more practical for daily commuters. It's far enough that most people should be able to make the school and work run multiple times without plugging in. It also makes them quite quick. The XC60 in plug-in T8 form gets to 60 mph from a standstill in 4.5 seconds, with the XC90 just 0.4 seconds behind.
Don't want something with a plug? Volvo will still offer the B5 flavor of the XC60, which has a mild hybrid setup offering 247 horsepower, 266 pound-feet of torque and an EPA rating of 26 MPG combined. The XC90 B5 also lives on, also with 247 horsepower, or there's a quicker B6 mild hybrid, with 295 hp.
Safety smarts
The XC60 also includes some other upgrades under the XC60's skin, including an updated sensor package. An additional radar sensor in the nose boosts this SUV's ability to detect obstacles ahead, while upgraded cameras look around the car in 360 degrees. It also includes an upgraded processor to aggregate all that data.
More safety smarts enables a new lane-change assist feature, where the car will automatically handle changes on the highway as directed by you. But there's also the promise of new features to come in the future thanks to over-the-air updates, another benefit of that new processor.
Interior tweaks
Inside, Volvo has recently upgraded the current XC60's interior with a bigger, still-vertical 11.2-inch display, and that carries over here. It still protrudes somewhat clumsily above the dashboard but gives you a few more inches to tap than the old display.
It's still a Google-powered interface, too, now augmented by Gemini, which means your idle AI conversations can continue in the car. Most importantly: Volvo didn't get rid of the volume knob, or any of the car's scant few remaining physical controls.
Subtle styling
All that's packaged up in some subtly revised bodywork. On the XC60, everything ahead of the front doors has been tweaked, including some new active-matrix LED headlights that can automatically dim individual sections, keeping the road illuminated without blinding oncoming traffic.
Volvo's designers revised the rear of the car as well. There's a new liftgate, bumper and LED taillights out back, though you'd be forgiven for not spotting the changes at a glance.
Volvo's SUVs are typically understated, but that's even more so with the 2028 XC60, which loses many creases, vents, and other bits of visual flair in pursuit of Scandinavian simplicity.
A familiar family hauler
For the new XC90, the visual changes are even more slight. In fact, there's only one: the new badge at the back that says Long Range, pointing to the additional miles offered by that uprated plug-in hybrid system.
Everything else is all carryover, which again isn't the end of the world given the current XC90 also already has the upgraded 11.2-inch display and the addition of Gemini.
Wrap-up
The net result of all that is a pair of SUVs that look much the same as they ever have, but now offer a much more compelling middle path between that comfortably familiar combustion lifestyle and going all-in on electrification. Of course, with the EX60 and EX90, Volvo's got you covered if you're feeling adventurous too.
What we don't know is how much extra you'll have to pay for that privilege. Right now, the 2026 Volvo XC60 T8 starts at $62,545, while the 2026 XC90 T8 is $77,595. Surely a significant boost in battery size will come with some extra cost, but we can't say for sure how much until we get closer to the release of both cars. If all goes well, they'll be hitting dealers in early 2027.

articles.title: OpenAI buys camera startup Glass Imaging for over $300m
articles.text:
OpenAI has bought Glass Imaging, a startup that uses AI to improve smartphone cameras, in a deal that values it at more than $300m. The Wall Street Journal reported the purchase on 14 September, citing people familiar with the matter.
According to the WSJ, OpenAI bought the company quietly in recent months. Neither company has announced the deal. OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment, TechCrunch reported.
A funding round last year valued Glass Imaging at about $100m, The Information reported, citing the WSJ. The reported price is more than three times that figure.
What Glass Imaging makes
Two former Apple engineers started the company in 2019, and it has its base in Los Altos, California. It had raised about $30m from investors before the deal, TechCrunch reported. Its website lists GV, LDV Capital, Future Ventures, Abstract Ventures, Ground Up, and Insight Partners as backers.
Its software, GlassAI, trains custom neural networks for each camera system. Glass Imaging says the software reverses “lens aberrations and sensor imperfections” to get more image quality out of existing hardware. The company describes its goal as bringing “DSLR quality to smartphones.”
The software works at the moment the shutter fires, rather than editing a photo afterwards, TechCrunch reported. In a 2024 funding announcement, the company cited DXOMARK tests of its software on the Motorola Edge 40 Pro. Honor also uses the technology in its phones, according to Tech Funding News.
Two former Apple engineers
Chief executive Ziv Attar and chief technology officer Tom Bishop both worked at Apple. Glass Imaging says Bishop co-created the technology behind the iPhone’s Portrait Mode. Attar founded LinX Imaging in 2011, which Apple bought in 2015, and later led computational photography work at Apple.
The deal drew congratulations from imaging researcher Peyman Milanfar. “The camera is the future of intelligence,” he wrote on X.
OpenAI’s hardware plans
OpenAI bought io, the device startup of former Apple design chief Jony Ive, for $6.5bn in 2025. Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, has since confirmed the company is building “a family of devices.”
Reports say its first device will be a screen-free smart speaker. Other reports say OpenAI is working on a phone built around AI agents, as well as earbuds. More than 200 employees work on its hardware, according to Tech Funding News.
Glass Imaging is the latest in a string of OpenAI acquisitions this year. Others include slide deck startup NextSlide and Northslope, which places engineers inside client businesses.

articles.title: Early Anthropic hire, former METR COO have found a way to rein in rogue AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A day after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job over concerns that AI could kill us all by the end of the decade, I met with founders and brothers-in-law Rune Kvist and Rajiv Dattani. They think they have a solution that could save us all, or at least help prevent AI agents from going rogue inside enterprises.
“AI is getting smarter at an increasingly rapid rate. The surprising thing about AI is that it becomes harder to adopt and harder to control as AI gets smarter, not easier,” said Kvist, an early Anthropic employee who is also married to Dattani’s sister). Dattani is the former COO of the AI safety research organization METR.
The pair launched a startup called Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company (AIUC) that hopes to bring AI safety to enterprises and companies building AI models and agents. The startup names Cursor, Lovable, Harvey, and ElevenLabs as customers.
On Tuesday, AIUC announced a $40 million Series A led by Ribbit Capital, with participation from First Harmonic. It previously closed a $15 million seed round from Nat Friedman through his fund NFDG, along with Emergence, Terrain, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann, among others, bringing its total funding to $55 million.
What caught the attention of this A-list group of investors is AIUC’s attempt to apply a familiar cybersecurity model to a new set of AI risks. The company has built a third-party audit and certification layer for AI agents.
“Banks, hospitals, governments and militaries no longer decline to deploy AI because a model isn’t smart enough,” Kvist said. “They decline because they’ve made commitments to their own customers about what a system will and won’t do, and nobody can currently guarantee that.”
Using the widely adopted cybersecurity standard SOC 2 as its muse, AIUC has developed a standard called AIUC-1 and a testing service to validate agents against the standard.
To build the standard, AIUC assembled a consortium of about 250 security and risk leaders — the buyers of agents. “These are the people who we meet with on a monthly basis, and the question we ask them is: When you’re buying agents from someone, what would you look for? What are the questions you’d want to ask, and what would you want to see addressed?” Dattani told TechCrunch.
That feedback shapes the tests. The startup then runs an agent through a suite of some 5,000 tests to see how it behaves in scenarios involving jailbreaks, hallucinations, and data leaks. The results produce a roughly 100-page report detailing where an agent performs safely and reliably — and where it doesn’t. Interestingly, AIUC uses AI agents to run the tests and AI to analyze the data. Humans, however, verify the final audit, Kvist said.
If this sounds a bit familiar, it is. Dattani’s former employer METR, where he was COO from 2024 to 2025 and remains a board member, does similar testing for the frontier labs, though its work until recently has focused mostly on performance (whether agents can reliably complete tasks). METR was one of the independent research orgs OpenAI used to investigate its Hugging Face incident.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also recently called for the AI industry to pace frontier development, citing a rapid increase in bad-behavior incidents. In his post, Amodei floated the idea of requiring frontier labs to use embedded third-party evaluators to observe and verify safety, and named METR as one possibility.
While AIUC isn’t proposing to embed itself at customer sites, the overall idea is similar: give enterprises an independent assessment of how safe their AI agents are. “Here’s where it passes and where you can trust it. And here’s where there’s concerns. You should be aware of those references before you make the decision to buy,” Dattani said.

articles.title: Fujifilm’s Instax Pal 2 is a tiny digital camera that may not disappoint
articles.text:
Fujifilm announced a follow-up to its tiny and quirky Instax Pal camera that debuted three years ago bundled with an instant printer. While the original Pal was a palm-sized camera with a round design that lacked a screen or viewfinder, the new Instax Pal 2 includes both in a design that looks like a miniaturized analog film camera. It’s also reminiscent of trendy pocket-friendly cameras like the Kodak Charmera, but with specs that may actually produce decent shots.
Fujifilm’s Instax Pal 2 is a tiny digital camera that may not disappoint
The $170 Pal 2 includes an LCD screen, a 10-megapixel sensor, autofocus, and face detection.
The Instax Pal 2 will launch in the US later this month for $169.95, according to PetaPixel, and uses a ⅓.06-inch sensor paired with an f/2.2 28mm lens to capture images up to 10-megapixels in size. That’s a big step up over the Kodak Charmera’s 1.6-megapixel sensor. The Pal 2 has an optical viewfinder and a 1.3-inch LCD screen on top for framing shots and is equipped with autofocus capabilities including optional face detection plus adjustable ISO, shutter speed, and exposure compensation.
Atop the Instax Pal 2 you’ll find a shutter button, a joystick, and a functional lever similar to what old film cameras used to advance to the next exposure. The camera pairs with Fujifilm’s mobile app where you can select and download image effects to the Pal 2 or upload images to your phone for printing using a wireless Bluetooth connection or a slide-out USB-C port. The camera also features a flash, a tripod mount, a self-timer, and a rechargeable battery good for up to three hours of use, Fujifilm claims.

articles.title: CCTV Script 15/09/26
articles.text:
– This is the script of CNBC's financial news report for China's CCTV on SEPTEMBER 15, 2026.
I am live on Silicon Valley's famed Sand Hill Road, home to a heavy concentration of private equity, venture capital, and private credit firms. Over the past decade, the US private capital market expanded rapidly, with private credit emerging as an increasingly essential financing channel outside traditional banking. Yet as the Federal Reserve potentially re-enters a rate-hiking cycle, this trillion-plus dollar market faces a fresh stress test.
As inflation expectations heat up, the 10-year US Treasury yield has once again touched the critical 5% threshold.
Market pricing from the CME FedWatch Tool now indicates that the probability of a 25 basis point rate hike by the Fed in September has surpassed 90%.
Former Federal Reserve Bank of New York President Bill Dudley told CNBC that given current market expectations, a failure to hike by the Fed would surprise markets and potentially damage its credibility. JPMorgan similarly views the likelihood of a rate hike as significantly elevated.
JACK CAFFREY
Portfolio Manager
J.P. Morgan
"I think that's the most likely outcome. I go back to my fixed income colleagues who continue to tell me the Fed refuses to surprise the bond market. We'll have to see if that will hold to be true. But when you look at what futures are indicating, I think there's a certain high confidence in terms of seeing a hike right now."
If the Federal Reserve indeed delivers a 25 basis point hike as markets expect, does it signal that the Fed has initiated a new rate-hiking cycle? Current market tracking data shows that the probability of the Fed executing cumulative rate hikes of at least 50 basis points by December has approached 80%.
In other words, markets are not only betting that the Fed will resume rate hikes, but also pricing in a high likelihood of at least two rate increases before year-end. This threatens to intensify debt repayment pressures across credit markets. Bloomberg, citing the latest data from rating agency Fitch, noted that the default rate in the US private credit market over the past 12 months has climbed to a record high of 6.3%. Among smaller corporate borrowers with annual operating profits below 25 million dollars, the default rate has reached 12.0%. Over the past decade, the US private credit market expanded rapidly, swelling from roughly 200 billion dollars in 2012 to over 1.5 trillion dollars today. Because a vast portion of these loans carry floating rates, renewed rate hikes by the Fed at a time when defaults are already at record levels could further escalate debt servicing pressures for highly leveraged enterprises.
The Federal Reserve Banks of New York and Dallas launched dedicated surveys targeting the private credit market for the first time this year. We will continue to track whether the spillover effects of future rate hikes further transmit into credit markets.

articles.title: Why de-dollarization discussions are more talk, less action
articles.text:
When BRICS leaders met over the weekend, they talked about the economic power of the Global South and the need to expand trade in local currencies, signaling a push to cut dependence on the greenback.
The bloc aims to reduce its reliance on the greenback due to geopolitical tensions, economic sanctions, and the U.S. tariff policy, experts said. However, they raised doubts about the ability of the BRICS to wean away from the dollar.
For years, the term "de-dollarization" has come up from time to time, especially when confidence in the U.S. is shaken.
The idea is simple: Countries mostly transact in the U.S. dollar today, thereby underpinning most of the world's financial systems. For example, two of the world's most traded commodities, oil and gold, are denominated in the greenback. 
Data from the Bank of International Settlements reveals that the U.S. dollar made up 89% of the forex market — up 1 percentage point from a year earlier —  while the euro and the yen made up 29% and 17%, respectively, as of April.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said in his address at the BRICS Summit that BRICS should "press ahead with greater use of local currencies, stronger cross-border payment systems and deeper financial interconnectivity."
Energy-rich economies such as Iran and Russia, two members of the BRICS, whose ability to trade in dollars has been hampered due to U.S. sanctions, also urged the bloc to develop payment, settlement and depository infrastructure within BRICS.
The current financial system is "vulnerable to political shocks due to its concentration on a limited number of currencies," Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, hinting at the need to diversify away from the dollar.
Yet lack of financial and macroeconomic integration, wide trade imbalances and deep distrust between key member states, such as China and India, are the biggest hurdles the BRICS need to cross before it breaks free from the hegemony of the dollar, experts said.
The BRICS lack the unified institutional, financial, and macroeconomic infrastructure needed to substitute the "inherent liquidity and trust" of the dollar globally, Jayant Krishna, senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.
Baby steps
The most common mention of de-dollarization is usually among the BRICS countries. U.S. President Donald Trump has in the past threatened the bloc with tariffs if they moved away from the dollar.
"We require a commitment from these Countries that they will neither create a new BRICS Currency, nor back any other Currency to replace the mighty U.S. dollar, or they will face 100% Tariffs and should expect to say goodbye to selling into the wonderful U.S. Economy," Trump wrote.
Collectively, 10 BRICS member countries accounted for 27% of world output, 24% of merchandise exports, and 22% of foreign direct investment inflows in 2024, a United Nations Trade and Development report said in March.
"This brings fresh opportunities, avenues for cooperation and vast potential," the report said but underscored that at present the scale of intra-BRICS trade only accounted for about 5% of world trade as of 2024.
While member countries have spoken of expanding trade in national currencies, few concrete steps have been seen in that direction. The BRICS 2026 declaration had no mention of common currency or firmer details on trade settlements and investments using BRICS local currencies. Instead, the BRICS Payment Task Force was asked to work on facilitating "practical solutions for cross-border payments."
"Russia and China now settle close to ninety percent of their trade in rubles and yuan," but that shift has been accelerated by U.S. sanctions after 2022 rather than coordinated BRICS policy, Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at Verisk Maplecroft, told CNBC
Most BRICS currencies lack deep liquid markets outside their home economies, which discourages exporters from accepting them and keeps dollar invoicing the path of least resistance for global commodities, she explained.
Experts said that competing interests among BRICS nations also make de-dollarization difficult.
China-India competition
"India-China rivalry, which I'd call the single biggest brake on cohesion across the bloc," Bhattacharya said.
Both Beijing and New Delhi want greater strategic autonomy from Washington, but they remain direct competitors in manufacturing, technology, investment and regional influence.
This tension, in addition to a widening trade imbalance between the two major BRICS countries, makes the trust needed for deeper financial integration hard to sustain.
China is one of India's largest business partners, with total trade at a record $151.1 billion in the year ending March 2026. But New Delhi's deficit with Beijing has also risen to a record $112.16 billion, up from $99.21 billion.
Meanwhile, India's goods and services trade with the U.S. was around $239 billion in 2025, with a goods trade surplus of $58.4 billion and a services trade surplus of $4.7 billion. So, a shift away from the dollar does not work in India's favor, as it has a large trade deficit with China and other countries.
"BRICS members also have vastly different priorities," Krishna Bhimavarapu, APAC Economist, State Street Investment Management, told CNBC.
Russia and Iran want to reduce dollar exposure because of sanctions risk; China wants greater international use of the renminbi but maintains capital controls; India, meanwhile, supports greater use of the rupee, he said.
"Ultimately, no BRICS-led alternative currently matches the liquidity and market depth, credibility and global acceptance of the Dollar," he added.

articles.title: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff joins growing chorus of tech leaders warning about AI risks
articles.text:
Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff on Tuesday became the latest tech leader to urge the artificial intelligence industry to act responsibly as increasingly powerful models become more widely used.
His comments come amid an intensifying debate over AI safety, fueled most recently by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's weekend essay calling for frontier AI labs to slow the pace of model development to give safety measures more time to catch up.
Benioff has a history of imploring tech companies to think of the greater good. For years, he's been an outspoken critic of social media companies and their impact on society, declaring in 2018 that "Facebook is the new cigarettes," and calling for greater government regulation of the industry.
Now, he is warning AI companies not to repeat the same mistakes. "A lot of companies got hurt, a lot of individuals got hurt through social media," Benioff told Jim Cramer in a "Mad Money" interview from the sidelines of his company's annual Dreamforce event in San Francisco. "We don't want that to happen in AI."
The warning is particularly notable given Salesforce's deep ties to the companies at the forefront of the AI boom. Last month, Salesforce unveiled Claudeforce, which includes a plugin allowing clients to use Anthropic's Claude to tap customer data stored in Salesforce and perform tasks such as composing emails and updating records. On Tuesday, Amodei appeared on stage during Benioff's keynote address and said, "I think that's the way to lead the industry forward, to set an example, to say that everyone can always be better."
Benioff has stopped short of criticizing AI companies or endorsing calls to slow AI development. Instead, he argued that companies building the technology have a responsibility to consider its broader consequences as they push ahead. "We want AI to take care of these things and be held responsible, and take care of these actions and be ethical," Benioff said. "The heart of ethics is responsibility."
He added, "We really look at a light on our brethren here in San Francisco and all over the world and say, 'We want you to be ethical in your actions and how you take care of your communities and the world,' because this technology is very powerful."
Salesforce shares on Tuesday gave back some of their more than 4.5% advance from the prior session. Enterprise software stocks soared Monday on Amodei's call to slow down AI development. The group, which was crushed earlier this year on AI disruption fears, has been making a comeback over the past few months as Wall Street warms to the idea that AI can't replace everything. Salesforce is up more than 50% from its 52-week low of $146 in late June. The stock has been a long-time holding in the CNBC Investing Club portfolio.

articles.title: Nvidia's Huang rips Anthropic's proposal for AI safety antitrust waiver: 'Completely unnecessary'
articles.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Tuesday slammed proposals of artificial intelligence companies antitrust exemptions that could coordinate a slowdown of developing increasingly powerful models.
Huang's comments — in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer — come during an intense debate over AI safety fueled by an essay Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published Saturday. Amodei proposed that leading AI labs coordinate to "pace the frontier," or deliberately slow the development of advanced models to give companies more time to test and safeguard. Amodei said that effort could require government mediation or waivers of antitrust restrictions.
Huang agreed that AI companies need to take safety seriously, but argued they should be able to solve those challenges themselves.
"The fact that we need new laws, new antitrust laws, or new regulations, so that these companies could do their fundamental engineering and do it properly before they release products, that is just completely unnecessary," Huang said on CNBC's "Mad Money." "We have plenty of laws. We have plenty of regulations that govern the reliability and the functionality of products."
In his essay, Amodei laid out a three-step approach to moderate the pace of model development, beginning with embedding third-party safety evaluators at each lab. The second and third steps are democratic and global coordination on safety standards and "limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress," Amodei wrote. "Some forms of coordination that would be impactful for pacing are legally challenging, and will require government support."
The legal issues arise because leading AI labs are competitors and their models are competing products. The Sherman Antitrust Act generally prohibits agreements among rivals that unreasonably restrain competition, while certain forms of coordination — including agreements to restrict output — can be illegal. That creates potential legal risks if competing AI developers were to jointly agree on how quickly they would develop or release new models.
Huang said model developers have the power to ensure their products are safe before releasing them.
"Safety is an engineering problem. Testing is an engineering problem," said Huang, whose company counts Anthropic and rival lab OpenAI as important customers. Nvidia also develops its own Nemotron family of open-weight models. "We should create products and properly test them. And if they're not ready to be released, just hold on to it and keep testing it and keep engineering until it's ready."
The AI boom has turned Nvidia into the world's largest chipmaker and most valuable company. Efforts to slow the development of more capable models may pose a risk to Nvidia's future growth.
Anthropic did not respond to CNBC's request for comment on Huang's remarks.
"AI safety is a real thing," Huang told Cramer. "Engineering products so that they are safe for the world to use — that's a real thing. And companies should innovate as fast as possible, but they should never innovate so fast as to release unsafe products."
Huang also pushed back against warnings that increasingly powerful AI models will pose an existential threat to humanity.
"We're not going to die in 2030," he said. "There are so many people in the world who are going to build AI properly. We're going to have all kinds of guardrails, invent all kinds of technology for safety and security."
